articles.content: Vivienne Foroughirad/Texas A&M/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project In the turquoise waters of Western Australia’s Shark Bay lives a large resident population of dolphins. Some of these marine mammals are 54 years old, others just infants. But no matter their age, they live highly social lives. Researchers have studied these dolphins for decades . Forty years on, our extensive dataset reveals crucial insights into how these animals socialise throughout their lives – and how their social choices affect their health and fitness. In our new study , published in PLOS Biology, we analysed nearly 40 years of data on over 450 wild Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins ( Tursiops aduncus ) from Shark Bay. We found that as dolphins navigate their social world, they develop unique personalities and social preferences, and individuals who are consistent about these preferences may live longer. Sociality is a spectrum Dolphins’ social lives mirror our own in remarkable ways. As they navigate their blue world, dolphins move in and out of social groups, constantly making decisions about who to spend time with and who to avoid, depending on the task at hand. Much like humans, dolphins vary markedly in how social they are. Research shows some are more cliquish, while others are true social butterflies, embedded in large and complex social networks These differences matter. Just as in humans and many other species, the way dolphins navigate their social lives can shape their survival, longevity and reproductive success. For example, strong social connections promote resilience, while social isolation can increase mortality risk . Such patterns are not set in stone either. In many species , including humans, social behaviour is shaped as we age. In humans, social networks often become smaller, with older adults becoming more selective, investing their time and energy in a smaller number of meaningful relationships. But what happens as dolphins age? Previous research on dolphins has shown us that extended maternal care in older dolphin mothers is evidence of reproductive senescence – similar to menopause in humans. This raises an intriguing question: do dolphins also show other patterns of ageing like our own? Drone footage of six individuals who reside in nearshore habitat off the coast of Monkey Mia, Shark Bay. In front from left to right are Risotto (24) and her calf, Linguini (2), who is in a nursing position; Whoops (27), and Wags (6). Behind them are two more individuals; Risotto’s previous calf Arancini (6), and Jungle (8). Diana Alvarado/Shark Bay Dolphin Research Project , CC BY Social ageing can be measured in multiple ways As we age, we develop personalities, build and lose relationships, and create our unique social environment which changes with each passing year. This process of social change as we grow is called social ageing . Most studies of social ageing have examined how individuals change over time by collecting many measurements, then finding their average. This can be useful for dolphins that have only a few close companions. But for those who frequently join groups large and small, an average tells us very little. We can instead turn to another measurement: predictability . This describes the spread of an individual’s data. Those dolphins who consistently spend time with the same number of other dolphins are very predictable. Those who flit between groups of many sizes are much less predictable. Predictability is difficult to measure because it requires a single individual be measured dozens, even hundreds, of times. Luckily, with 40 years of data on over 450 dolphins, research can go beneath the surface to study not only how individuals change in sociability with age on average, but how predictable they are, and if predictability can change, too. Being consistent is key For our new study, we examined the effects of sex, age, and individual personality on group size (a measure of sociability) throughout the population of dolphins at Shark Bay. We discovered several key points. First, dolphins follow a pattern very similar to humans and other long-lived species: they increase their average group size with age, to a point. After that point, which is unique to each individual, those average group sizes begin to decrease. Second, regardless of what their average group size is, individuals become more predictable with age. Third, males had a higher average group size and higher predictability than females. Finally, individuals who continued to increase their group size average and predictability most with age lived longer. Social stability can being a sustaining force Our research into dolphins’ social lives suggests that developing a strong and stable social environment can buffer many of the effects of ageing and enhance lifespan. Studying dolphins’ social traits reveals that it’s not only average behaviour which shapes fitness outcomes, but individual predictability. To truly understand how ageing shapes us, we must look beyond the average to see how the predictability of our social decisions can affect us as we navigate our world. This study reinforces the importance of maintaining consistent social relationships throughout the ageing process. In the case of the Shark Bay dolphins, it’s not only about how large one’s social circle is; rather, it’s about the social circle staying roughly the same size and type over size. And this holds an important lesson for us, because the trends we find in dolphins closely parallel the sort of patterns we see in human social behaviour as well. This project has received grant funding from the National Science Foundation and the US Office of Naval Research, as well as material support from the Royal Automobile Club Monkey Mia Resort. articles.content: Australia is currently in talks with the European Space Agency (ESA) over potentially flying Katherine Bennell-Pegg on a future space mission. If accepted, Bennell-Pegg – who is the director of space technology at the Australian Space Agency and completed ESA training in 2024 – would become the first officially funded Australian astronaut. To “buy a seat” on a space mission, Australia has to make a financial contribution to the ESA. The precise sum is not public, but reports claim it could exceed the A$100 million mark . There has been interest in the press and excitement among space advocates. Many are pointing out that sending a home-grown astronaut to space would yield potential benefits to industry and the nation as a whole, inspiring younger generations. There would be a powerful symbolism in sending an Australian woman to space. However, while human spaceflight can deliver substantial benefits, it’s costly. As we’re in the midst of a substantial public campaign to #FlyKatherine , it’s crucial to properly analyse some of the claims being made about the potential benefits of such an expensive proposal. What counts as an Australian astronaut? The discussion raises an interesting point about what constitutes an Australian astronaut. To date, five Australian-born people have flown to space, two as NASA astronauts and three privately. The most recent was physicist Elaine Hyde, the first Australian woman in space . But her 2025 Blue Origin flight was privately funded, and she hasn’t been given the label of the first “female Australian astronaut”. The federal government hasn’t signalled a strong interest in flying an Australian astronaut. Science minister Tim Ayres unequivocally said state and territory governments and private industry would have to pitch in. However, only South Australia has agreed to contribute; industry has pledged up to $6 million. The Northern Territory called the proposal “ reckless ”. These debates are not new. In the 1980s, the Hawke government announced it would send an Australian astronaut on the space shuttle. However, then Minister for Science, Barry Jones, noted it wasn’t a high priority . Prestige and public relations were not considered reason enough when government spending was to be reined in. The cost would be substantial We don’t know if Australians would support spending $100m on a single space mission while facing a cost-of-living crisis. When surveyed in 2025, 51.5% of Australians supported government investment in an astronaut programme, but respondents were not given a cost. Generally speaking, once government programs reveal their costs , public support decreases. When asked in 2023 , more Australians supported the cancellation of a $1.2 billion Earth observation satellite than disagreed with it being canned. Would these funds be better deployed within the space sector? Currently the Australian Space Agency’s funding is $21.7m over two years. The cost of flying a single Australian astronaut would fund a decade for the agency. Put another way, $100m is half of the total government investment in space or space adjacent companies in the last 18 months. Space science and research occurs at universities, in government agencies, and in private industry; many organisations have sent experiments to space, often relatively cheaply. Advocates have argued there would be significant benefits to Australia. There’s no doubt space is of immense benefit to industry and the nation, from banking to navigation to farming . An astronaut can’t meet all these needs, and we don’t know how they fit into our long-term plans. Australia doesn’t have a whole of government space policy and an astronaut is not a space program. The suggestion that Australia’s growing space industry would stand to gain similarly deserves deeper analysis. How and where specifically will funds flow back to Australia? Does the public think supporting industry is a reason to send an astronaut to space? ESA has a geographic return policy which sees member states receive industrial contracts proportional to how much they pay ESA. But Australia is not a paying member state, and not looking to be. The $100 million includes training, equipment and launch; it’s difficult to see how the bulk of those funds will be spent in Australia rather than in Europe, where ESA is based. What about inspiration? Representation matters, particularly for encouraging girls and young women to pursue careers in space. Bennell-Pegg’s selection and training have already inspired Australians across the country. However, research shows that when role models in STEM (science, technology, engineering, mathematics) fields have seemingly unattainable careers, they actually make students less motivated to pursue STEM. The selection process was not nationally competitive and there’s no currently published plan or pathway for a young girl in Australia to follow in Bennell-Pegg’s footsteps. What message does that send to young people? It might discourage them from pursuing careers in space. We shouldn’t ignore the fact many Australians would support sending an astronaut simply because it’s exciting. That is a legitimate foundation for policy – after all we fund the arts, entertainment industry and sport – but we should also recognise many Australians would not agree with such spending when it comes to space. Unanswered questions remain If we want to send an astronaut to space, the Australian public should know precisely what the tangible benefits are – to them, their economy and their sense of what Australia stands for. A key final question is: what next? There are currently no plans for Australia to send a second astronaut to space after Bennell-Pegg. Not only does this limit the pathway for future Australians to go to space, but also undermines the arguments put forward for an Australian astronaut. If the benefits are so tangible and important, we wouldn’t only do it once. Kathryn Robison receives funding from the Department of Defence and is the Deputy President of Women In International Security Australia Inc. (WIIS-A). Tristan Moss receives funding from the Australian Research Council and the Department of Defence.

articles.content: The Australian government has secured an agreement with the Greens to guarantee passage of its long-awaited digital duty of care bill . The bill puts the onus on big-tech companies to address foreseeable online harms. Announced on Tuesday, the deal includes a number of measures to strengthen the bill, including bigger fines for platforms (to as much as 5% of global revenue) and a private right for people to sue the companies that breach their duty of care. Federal Minister for Communications Anika Wells acknowledged that it’s impossible to “cure” the internet of its ills. But she emphasised the digital duty of care bill provides basic safety standards that have to date been lacking. She described the package as “ seismic reform ”. What exactly is a ‘digital duty of care’? At its core, the bill requires the person responsible for an online service to ensure – as much as is reasonably practicable – a safe online environment . That phrase is borrowed from workplace health and safety law, and the logic is similar: rather than waiting for harmful content to be reported and taken down, platforms must identify the risks their services create and act to reduce them. The duty replaces the existing industry codes – which Wells described as “ drafted by big tech for big tech ” – as well as the eSafety Commissioner’s Basic Online Safety Expectations . Under the new bill, platforms would have to complete annual written risk assessments, keep them for six years and produce them to the eSafety Commissioner on request. The legislation has been years in the making. A statutory review of the Online Safety Act, delivered in October 2024, made 67 recommendations to strengthen the law. Its central one was a single, overarching “duty of care”, which the government committed to. After nearly two years, the government released an exposure draft in September, the headline feature of which was an “ off switch ” for personalised, algorithm-driven feeds for users. The bill was introduced to parliament on October 15. A Senate committee then reviewed the bill, receiving 182 submissions. Last week, it released its recommendations, which included a civil right of action and an exemption for low-risk services, such as small business websites. It backed passage of the bill, subject to its recommendations. What are the new changes? Wells outlined seven new changes to the bill as part of the government’s deal with the Greens: a private right of action, allowing individuals and groups to sue platforms that breach the duty stronger privacy protections expanded powers for eSafety to remove nudify services the naming of addictive platform design features as a specific risk that platforms must assess a clarified definition of “hostile attitudes to women”, which Wells said targets content promoting hatred, violence and threats, not disagreement with feminism a rule-making power to create an external dispute resolution pathway higher fines for violations of the law. The penalty change is the headline amendment. The bill already carried a maximum penalty of about A$109 million for companies found to have breached the obligation. The amendment adds an alternative penalty of up to 5% of global revenue. Among jurisdictions with similar laws, this would place Australia between Canada at 3% and the European Union at 6%. The Greens had sought 10% . The dispute resolution pathway is what the Greens call a pathway to an independent ombudsman for big tech. It creates a three-tiered option for social media users to bring complaints of harms against tech companies. First, they can turn to the platforms’ internal complaint process. If that fails, they can complain to a yet-to-be established tech platform ombudsman. Then if that fails, they can use the private right of action to go to court. The duty of care law would go into force after a 12-month transition. The government has confirmed low-risk, small businesses will be exempted from the law through rules, rather than in the bill itself. A significant shift There are several reasons why the changes to the bill are significant. First, the private right of action changes who enforces the law. Until now, online safety regulation in Australia has depended almost entirely on the eSafety Commissioner’s resources and priorities. A statutory duty that individuals and groups of people can use to sue means platforms face litigation risk, as well as regulatory risk. That matters because suing platforms has been difficult. For example, Australian mining magnate Andrew Forrest’s case against Meta over scam advertisements had to be pursued in a US court. Wells argued that Australians have previously had to attach claims to existing laws in order to sue. The new law would create a cause of action that does not currently exist. However, she said she expects it to be used rarely. Much will depend on how the courts approach causation in these types of cases, and on whether those financially backing litigation see class actions against platforms as viable. Second, the revenue-based fine raises the stakes with Washington. Wells said she met the US ambassador on Tuesday morning and acknowledged “points of difference” on this clause. She noted that courts elsewhere have rarely imposed maximum penalties against companies. The 5% figure is a ceiling, not a starting point. Third, the politics have changed. The Coalition opposes the bill, and Wells noted it will be the first online safety law to pass without bipartisan support. Online safety has been a rare area of consensus in Australia in the past. If the Coalition votes against the law, it is more exposed to being unwound, or simply under-resourced, after a change of government. Much of the detail is still to come. The dispute resolution scheme, the small business exemption and the treatment of addictive design all depend on rules yet to be written and on eSafety’s judgement. Regardless, with the passage of the bill now secured, the duty of care will shift responsibility to the companies that build these services. Rob Nicholls is a member of the University of Sydney Centre for AI, Trust, and Governance. He receives funding from the ARC. He made a submission to, and appeared before, the Senate committe.

articles.content: Irina/Getty Images Have you ever wondered why restaurants include outrageously expensive bottles of wine on their menus? Often, those bottles aren’t expected to sell. Instead, they make the other wines seem better value even if they are still overpriced. By changing the context of the decision, the out-of-reach expensive option can nudge customers towards wanting the cheaper option more. Marketers use similar tricks all the time. A holiday package that’s sold out, a premium subscription nobody really wants, or a product that’s clearly overpriced can all influence how we perceive the alternatives around them. Behavioural economists call these influences “decoy effects” . They reveal that decisions are not always rational based on absolute value. Instead, they are often shaped by the options available at the time. Humans aren’t the only animals making decisions. Every day, wild animals weigh up risks and rewards: whether to investigate a novel object, where to forage, or whether entering a trap is worth the potential danger. That got us wondering: could a decoy influence a rat? That was the subject of our new study, published today in The Journal of Applied Ecology . The problem with trapping rats Rats are among the world’s most successful and adaptable animals. They damage crops and infrastructure, spread disease, threaten native wildlife and cost economies billions of dollars every year in damages and pest control. Despite more than a century of innovation and thousands of patented trap designs, trapping still depends on one crucial step: the animal must choose to enter the trap. This seemingly simple decision is often where pest control programs fail. Many rats are naturally cautious around unfamiliar objects, a behaviour known as neophobia . A trap may contain attractive food, but if the perceived risk outweighs the reward, a rat may simply refuse to enter. Researchers and pest managers have traditionally tried to solve this problem by improving lures, making traps more appealing, or reducing fear of the trap itself. We explored a different possibility. Instead of changing the trap, could we change the rat’s perception of its options? An irresistible snack just out of reach To test this idea, we worked with wild black rats ( Rattus rattus ) in bushland around Sydney. We set up tracking tunnels which work much the same way as traps but the animals are free to leave. Outside some of the tunnel entrances, we placed a highly desirable peanut butter bait ball inside a steel mesh container. Rats could see and smell the peanut butter, but they couldn’t eat it. In effect, we created a “phantom decoy” – a tempting option that was present but unattainable. The idea was borrowed directly from behavioural economics. If the highly desirable but inaccessible food changed how rats perceived the available food inside the tunnel, rats might be more willing to enter. A surprising result The results were striking. Rats were 83% more likely to enter tunnels containing a basic food reward when the inaccessible “phantom” food was present. To our knowledge, this is the first evidence that a “phantom decoy” effect, a phenomenon well documented in human decision-making , can be used to influence trap-entry behaviour in a wild mammal. The decoy itself could never be eaten. Yet its mere presence changed the rats’ decision-making behaviour. Importantly, our experimental controls showed that placing the same inaccessible food inside the tunnel didn’t increase entry rates, nor was the effect simply due to the extra food attracting more rats to the area. The increase in tunnel entry only happened when the inaccessible food was positioned outside the tunnel, suggesting it changed how rats evaluated the option of entering. This suggests rats weren’t simply responding to the amount of food available. Instead, their decisions were influenced by how the options were presented. While we can’t know exactly how a rat experiences these choices, the findings show that altering perceived alternatives can substantially influence how rats behave. What this could mean for pest control The practical implications are potentially significant. Pest managers often encounter animals that investigate traps or bait stations but refuse to enter. This problem occurs at every scale , from failed island eradications to backyard rats that seem impossible to catch. When lures alone aren’t enough to overcome an animal’s reluctance to enter, changing how it perceives its options may be an effective alternative. Our study suggests a relatively simple and inexpensive way to encourage animals to enter traps: add a highly desirable but inaccessible food option outside the trap entrance. Importantly, this approach doesn’t require a new trap design, sophisticated technology or costly equipment. It simply changes the decision-making environment. Beyond rats The findings also raise a broader question. For decades, behavioural economists and psychologists have documented decision-making biases in humans. Increasingly, evidence suggests that some of these principles may extend beyond our own species. Animals, like humans, constantly make choices under uncertainty. Understanding those choices could unlock new ways to manage pest species , conserve threatened wildlife and improve animal monitoring. Sometimes, the best way to get an animal to choose option A may not be to make option A better. It may be to add option B. articles.content: ChiccoDodiFC / Getty Images On Friday, Turkish-American mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge announced he had produced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most important and famous open problems in mathematics, with the aid of an artificial intelligence (AI) model. Alpöge – a prominent figure in AI-assisted mathematics – announced the result via a four-page statement on his website . In it, he describes the Riemann hypothesis as “the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood”. He also notes that he wanted to publish earlier, but delayed because there was “a constraint to respect” – presumably commercial rules around Anthropic’s share market listing last week, which raised over US$100 billion. The claimed proof is the latest in a deluge of significant AI-assisted mathematical discoveries announced over the past six months, as AI companies turn their vast resources on one of humanity’s great intellectual activities as a testing ground. What is the Riemann hypothesis? First posed by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis is about a mathematical object called the Riemann zeta function (often written ζ( s )). This function is important in number theory because it is related to how prime numbers are distributed. It can be used to estimate how many prime numbers exist that are smaller than any given number. In essence, the Riemann hypothesis says that all “non-trivial” solutions of the equation ζ( s ) = 0 – the “zeroes” of the zeta function – must be on a particular vertical straight line. Alpöge’s proof actually claims to prove the broader claim known as the generalised Riemann hypothesis, likely first posed around 1884, which extends the idea to a bigger family of functions that are connected to many parts of number theory. Have people tried to prove it before? Over the past century and a half, there have been many attempts to prove the Riemann hypothesis and its generalisations. In 1900, German mathematician David Hilbert listed it in his influential collection of 23 problems for the 20th century. In 2000, the Clay Mathematics Institute offered million-dollar prizes for solving seven key problems for the 21st century, and again a proof of the Riemann hypothesis was on the list. The hypothesis has been formulated in more than 100 equivalent ways . More than 12 trillion zeroes of the function have been checked and found to be on the critical line. But still, a proof that all the zeroes must be on that line has been elusive. Is this a better way to publish AI-assisted maths results? Over the past year, mathematicians have grown accustomed to AI companies releasing significant results in unceremonious dumps . Many high-profile discoveries have been announced with much fanfare. But behind the splashes have been seemingly unvetted and unedited AI-produced manuscripts. This offloads responsibility for actually checking the results onto the mathematical community, which has caused a great deal of discontent. Alpöge’s claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis has felt a little different. Instead, he has described part of his process working with a large language model as a collaborator. He outlines some of the ideas that make the proof work, and gives a timeline of how the key parts of the proof developed. The proof itself was published as more than 17 million lines of code in the mathematical formalisation software Lean, rather than in a human-readable form. Lean allows a proof to be written in a way that lets a computer check each step of the argument and verify it as correct. Alpöge’s justification for the Lean-only release was that “[t]he argument is incredibly long”. He said his attempts at an AI-produced explanation in English “hit 250,000+ pages”, and it was “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop’”. So is the proof correct? Does this mean the hypothesis has definitively been proven? Not quite. There may be problems with how a proof is formalised, and mathematicians generally agree that a Lean formalisation alone is not enough to confirm a proof. That said, Alpöge’s proof is looking good. The Lean Focused Research Organization and the MathLib community that develops and maintains Lean and its mathematical libraries released a joint statement stating their belief in the correctness of the proof. Canadian mathematician Daniel Litt described the odd situation in this way: (1) The Lean-formalized proof of the Riemann hypothesis is exceedingly likely to be correct. (2) No human understands it yet. What about human mathematicians? Hot on the heels of Alpöge’s claim was a hurried announcement by Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society. He released another proposed proof of the generalised Riemann hypothesis – this one by Stanford mathematician Alessandro Maria Masullo. Vakil characterised Masullo’s proof, presented in a 940-page manuscript entitled The Music of the Primes, as “all human, with no AI”. The proof was still being checked when it was released, and potential problems had been found within hours of publication. It remains to see whether these can be corrected. In Alpöge’s announcement, he was careful to give praise and credit to a variety of mathematicians and colleagues. This goes against a noticeable trend in which AI-written papers do little to cite earlier work. Alpöge also indicates he will endeavour “to understand and impart understanding of this argument and its certain simplifications, to speak about it, to write it properly”. In the coming years, this remarkable mathematical achievement will no doubt be discussed and dissected, and the proof made comprehensible to humans. This discovery may also provide one of the first good examples of how AI-assisted breakthroughs can be announced and shared in a way that respects the mathematical community. articles.content: COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey, arriving for the final plenary meeting. Mike Muzurakis/IISD/ENB , CC BY-SA After stretching almost two days overtime, the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed after countries failed to agree on an overarching deal to combat climate change. The breaking point was a draft text with no mention of a phase-out of fossil fuels. Nearly 40 countries, including those in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama and vulnerable Pacific island nations such as Vanuatu and the Marshall Islands, formally objected to the final text. EU representatives called a climate deal that ignored phasing out fossil fuels “ unconscionable ”. But the summit also failed to deliver on several other significant issues. It was billed as the “implementation COP”, but delivered very few of the goals set by its co-presidents, Turkey and Australia. The rejection of the final text centred on other interrelated concerns : a lack of response to science that shows the world is about to breach 1.5°C of warming and inadequate financing for developing countries to respond to climate change. The aim was to triple adaptation financing to US$120 billion a year . That figure is now off the table, even though adaptation needs in the Global South alone are estimated at around US$500 billion a year . Talks about a just transition mechanism also made little progress. Even the goal for clean electricity to supply 35% of the world’s energy use by 2035 was only supported as a voluntary pledge by 90 countries. Science in the firing line I attended the summit in my role as chair of the World Climate Research Programme . My job, alongside other UN agencies, was to make sure the best available science underpinned the negotiations. It was disheartening to watch how hard that science was fought. The International Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) delivers its major reports every six or seven years and is currently working on its latest assessment. In between, the UN Environmental Programme’s ( UNEP ) annual Emissions Gap and Adaptation Gap reports and the World Meteorological Organization ’s State of the Global Climate report show how far off track nations are from meeting commitments made under the Paris Agreement. According to UNEP’s recent “overshoot” report and the 2026 Global Carbon Budget report , the world will reach 1.5°C of long-term warming around 2030. This breaches the lower limit of the Paris Agreement. For small island states and the least developed countries, the 1.5°C line is existential and non-negotiable. For the first time, COP31 discussed the concept of overshoot and how warming could be brought back down to 1.5°C again. This discussion split the room. Petrostates argued for carbon capture and removal, but at a scale that does not yet exist. Saudi Arabia, India and Russia, and at times China, discredited rigorously peer-reviewed findings. Small island states, meanwhile, refused any backsliding. Delay tactics Another flashpoint was an attempt to wave away the annual science reports altogether. Saudi Arabia, India and Russia objected to citing any findings other than the IPCC assessments, dismissing annual reports as “grey literature”. Meetings and press conferences were hastily convened, where I and other scientists behind these reports had to set out just how robust they are. The biggest fight of the summit was over the timing of the IPCC’s next major report, its Seventh Assessment Report . The above countries were accused of pushing for a delay until 2029. Read more: Why fossil fuel-producing countries are stalling this crucial climate report Dozens of European, African and Pacific nations want the report delivered earlier so it can inform the 2028 Global Stocktake when the world will measure its progress against the Paris Agreement goals. Pushing back the science until after the stocktake is a way of making sure the reckoning has nothing to measure against. The COP31 summit’s worth will be remembered for its outcome. Organisers will have to weigh the enormous cost and carbon footprint of flying in 92,000 people against the failure to agree on a final text. I cannot help asking whether these summits have had their day, and whether a new model is needed now. Climate change will not wait for the negotiators. If the system built to act on the science cannot even agree to hear it on time, we must find one that will. Tim Naish receives funding from the Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment. He chairs the Joint Scientific Committee of the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) and attended COP31 on a World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) badge as a climate science expert.

articles.content: Chi Pham/Unsplash Flowers have long been treasured by people in different cultures , depicted in magnificent works of art, and collected as cut flowers. Cut flowers can brighten our homes, decor and spirits. They often look great when we buy or collect them. But all too soon they are way past their best and look bedraggled in a murky vase. But we can use our knowledge of flowers to prolong their vase life for days, maximising their value and our enjoyment. A matter of exquisite timing Many flowers are bright, almost gaudy – and they have to be. They are all about attracting the mammals, birds and insects that pollinate them and make their reproduction successful. Plants need to produce flowers when environmental conditions are right, when the pollinators that they rely upon are out and about, and when the production and dispersal of seed are at an optimum. For most plants getting the timing right requires an accurate and reliable biological clock . When flowers are cut, the flow of water through their stems ceases. The water is vital in maintaining the water content of the cells of the stem and the flowers which are essentially pumped up like tiny balloons. All these fully inflated (or turgid) cells give the stem and floral structures strength. If the water supply is disrupted, water still evaporates from the floral parts and the whole structure starts to collapse or wilt. If air gets into the flower stems, it acts as a blockage and so wilting occurs faster. When flowers are cut, the flow of water through their stems ceases. Irina Donskaia/Unpslash Tips to make cut flowers last longer There are some simple, little things you can do to ensure that your cut flowers will look their best and remain fresh for as long as possible . 1. Choose the best First, gather or buy your flowers when they’re just about at their best and just before you want to place them in your vase. Open flowers should look in full bloom and colour and be upright. Buds should be plump and ready to open and they will open if your treat your flowers well and keep the water up to them. Do not leave them lying about with your shopping or in your car – especially in the warmer months. If you’re gathering your own flowers, cut the stems long, using sharp, clean secateurs. You can trim to length at home later. 2. Prepare for presentation Make sure your vase is nice and clean after any previous use. Always cut off at least the bottom two to three centimetres of the stem before you put the flower in the vase. If you can cut under water, do so. You do not want air to enter the water conducting vessels of the stem, as this causes a blockage. Remove wilting or rotting flowers that might be in the bunch. These can be a source of disease which can destroy plant tissues and allow air into the structure which would not enter a healthy plant if you have cut the stem correctly. Remove any lower leaves as you do not want them in the water, as they are more prone to rotting than the intact stems. Making the final cut at a 45 degree angle increases the surface area of the stem for greater water uptake. It seems to make little difference for narrow stemmed flowers, such as fresias, cosmos or lisianthus. But it’s worth doing for broader stemmed flowers, such as dahlias, some of the rose varieties and larger lilies. 3. Change the water regularly Change the water regularly – but do not expose the base of the stems to air. The simplest way of doing this is to tip out about 80% of the water and top up. A daily change is best but every couple of days is worthwhile. It provides fresh clean water for the flowers, prevents cloudiness and smells, and reduces the chance of bacterial and fungal growth. 4. Feed your flowers There are various additives you can place in the water to sustain the cut flowers and prolong their vase life. Adding a teaspoon of sugar can sustain the flowers as the sugar supplies extra carbohydrate and energy to the leaves and flowers, allowing them to function normally for longer. But it adds to the risk of bacterial and fungal contamination. If you do it, you must regularly change the water. You may need to top up the sugar if your flowers are lasting well. You do so by adding the right amount of sugar to the fresh water that you are adding. If you replace half the water, add half a teaspoon of sugar – add sugar in proportion to the fresh water that you are adding. If you add a little acid to you sugar mix, you can reduce the risk of contamination. A simple floral food formula is to mix 5ml (roughly a teaspoon) of vinegar and 5ml of sugar to 1 litre of water. You can use lemon juice rather than vinegar as they are both acidic. You can also add 2ml (half a teaspoon) of bleach as an antibacterial agent if you wish. This is a simple and balanced formula, but you should still change the water every 2–3 days. Many of the commercially available floral foods or the little sachets that some florists provide that you can buy from a nursery or that come in sachets at florists are similar mixes. Taking just a little extra care allows you to enjoy your cut flowers in full bloom for as long as possible. They are worth the effort and you make the most of a wonderful natural resource. articles.description: Chi Pham/Unsplash Flowers have long been treasured by people in different cultures , depicted in magnificent works of art, and collected as cut flowers. Cut flowers can brighten our homes, decor and spirits. They often look great when we buy or collect them. But all too soon they are way past their best and look bedraggled in a murky vase. But we can use our knowledge of flowers to prolong their vase life for days, maximising their value and our enjoyment. A matter of exquisite timing Many flowers are bright, almost gaudy – and they have to be. They are all about attracting the mammals, birds and insects that pollinate them and make their reproduction successful. Plants need to produce flowers when environmental conditions are right, when the pollinators that they rely upon are out and about, and when the production and dispersal of seed are at an optimum. For most plants getting the timing right requires an accurate and reliable biological clock . When flowers are cut, the flow of water through their stems ceases. The water is vital in maintaining the water content of the cells of the stem and the flowers which are essentially pumped up like tiny balloons. All these fully inflated (or turgid) cells give the stem and floral structures strength. If the water supply is disrupted, water still evaporates from the floral parts and the whole structure starts to collapse or wilt. If air gets into the flower stems, it acts as a blockage and so wilting occurs faster. When flowers are cut, the flow of water through their stems ceases. Irina Donskaia/Unpslash Tips to make cut flowers last longer There are some simple, little things you can do to ensure that your cut flowers will look their best and remain fresh for as long as possible . 1. Choose the best First, gather or buy your flowers when they’re just about at their best and just before you want to place them in your vase. Open flowers should look in full bloom and colour and be upright. Buds should be plump and ready to open and they will open if your treat your flowers well and keep the water up to them. Do not leave them lying about with your shopping or in your car – especially in the warmer months. If you’re gathering your own flowers, cut the stems long, using sharp, clean secateurs. You can trim to length at home later. 2. Prepare for presentation Make sure your vase is nice and clean after any previous use. Always cut off at least the bottom two to three centimetres of the stem before you put the flower in the vase. If you can cut under water, do so. You do not want air to enter the water conducting vessels of the stem, as this causes a blockage. Remove wilting or rotting flowers that might be in the bunch. These can be a source of disease which can destroy plant tissues and allow air into the structure which would not enter a healthy plant if you have cut the stem correctly. Remove any lower leaves as you do not want them in the water, as they are more prone to rotting than the intact stems. Making the final cut at a 45 degree angle increases the surface area of the stem for greater water uptake. It seems to make little difference for narrow stemmed flowers, such as fresias, cosmos or lisianthus. articles.content: After a string of major tech outages and incidents in the past week, it’s hard not to ask: is this really just a coincidence? Microsoft’s global outage last week disrupted email and business communications. A nationwide US aviation ground stop disrupted thousands of flights. Transaction problems at JPMorgan Chase affected the customers of other American banks. Apple suffered a services outage . Cyber criminals used legitimate third-party software Optimizely to plant malicious code on a slew of popular websites, including the BBC, CNN and Zoom. All within days. We know generative artificial intelligence (AI) has made sophisticated hacking tools increasingly available . So it makes sense to ask if these disparate incidents can be traced to AI-assisted cyber crime. However, what we know so far points to a more complex picture, with no simple solution. Were the recent tech incidents related? Despite it looking like the digital sky is falling, there’s no evidence the outages were related. But there does seem to be an underlying pattern of organisations patching and upgrading older systems . Microsoft’s preliminary investigation of its outage points to a software defect that remained hidden for months. US aviation authorities linked the ground stop to newly installed network equipment . Apple attributed its disruption to an internal update . On Wednesday, the US National Security Agency reported problems with its classified internal network , but said the outage happened during scheduled maintenance. Author provided The only cyberattack in the list is the Optimizely software being compromised . This online marketing platform, used by many major websites, was hijacked to steal customer payments and redirect about US$7,000 to cryptocurrency payment addresses, capture customer card details and exploit vulnerabilities in older iPhones. This actually shows that cyber criminals don’t always want to bring systems down. While millions struggled with failing digital services in the past week, a cyberattack quietly unfolded through trusted software on more than 170 websites. Why so many tech failures at once, then? Imagine a self-driving car that performs perfectly in a simulator, only to encounter unpredictable traffic, pedestrians and roadworks in a crowded city. Real roads are more complicated than any test environment. And a hidden defect can affect a whole fleet of vehicles at once, causing chaos. Modern digital systems – from aviation networks to banking to big tech suppliers like Microsoft – face the same challenge. Tech systems need updates for various reasons, from security patches and fixing bugs to introducing new features. And these updates are tested “offline” before engineers deploy them. However, an update to a system may pass every test, but behave differently across thousands of interconnected servers handling millions of requests. You might recall the massive Windows outage in mid-2024 that was traced back to a single software update. Automation can magnify these problems. Computers can deploy updates, monitor servers and redirect traffic without waiting for humans to intervene. The automation that allows companies to manage thousands of servers in minutes can also spread one mistake across thousands of servers in minutes. So how can we keep things running? The ability to keep essential services working through a disruption, whatever its cause, is known as operational resilience. Governments are beginning to act. Australia has sovereignty requirements for government data hosting (which means keeping some sensitive data onshore). In June, the government signed a digital resilience agreement with Microsoft , which means working with the tech giant more closely to address potential cyber risks as they come up. But such measures can’t keep essential services running while a global provider is down. Australia doesn’t need to build its own Microsoft or Google. Replicating these global platforms would be costly and complex, and wouldn’t guarantee freedom from outages. Returning to pen and paper isn’t an option either. Paper records can keep a pharmacy counter running for a few hours, but essential services now handle volumes of data that no manual system could absorb for long. Governments have a duty of care to keep essential services running. That means investing in what I call “targeted sovereign technological capabilities”, to allow select essential services to continue operating under disastrous conditions. This means establishing a minimal suite of options we can run locally. These would be pre-configured, regularly tested local systems that can keep the core functions of hospitals, emergency services and other critical areas running when global platforms such as Microsoft fail or are attacked. Regulators should require operators to test which critical functions they can carry out without their usual providers, and for how long, building on existing rules . We can do more Two further steps would help. First, Australia should have a say over how global providers roll out changes to their essential services, not merely be told about them. The rule should be universal: no single change should reach all of a nation’s essential services at once, with urgent security fixes the exception. Second, independent review shouldn’t stop at cyberattacks. Australia’s Cyber Incident Review Board examines significant cyber incidents, but almost every recent failure was declared not to be one, leaving the explanations to the companies themselves. articles.content: Cosminxp Cosmin Think about the last time you visited a website, created an online account or purchased something online. Chances are, at some point, you were asked to prove you were human. Perhaps you had to tick a box saying “I’m not a robot”, identify traffic lights or vehicles in a series of pictures, or complete a simple puzzle. These security checks, known as CAPTCHAs , have become a familiar part of our online experience. Most of us complete them without giving them much thought. Unfortunately, this test designed to protect us online can also be used to trick us into downloading malicious software (malware). What is CAPTCHA? Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart (CAPTCHA) is a security check that helps websites distinguish real people from automated computer programs, commonly known as bots. Bots now generate more web traffic than humans. According to the latest Thales Bad Bot Report , bots accounted for more than 53% of web traffic in 2025, up from 51% in 2024. A typical example of a CAPTCHA asking the user to identify objects. Google reCAPTCHA While many bots perform useful tasks, such as helping search engines discover websites, others are used to create fake accounts, send spam and attempt to break into online services. This is one reason websites use CAPTCHA checks to distinguish human visitors from automated programs and reduce malicious activity. Some ask us to identify objects, tick a checkbox or solve a puzzle. More advanced systems may also examine how someone interacts with a website to determine whether additional verification is needed. Beware the fake CAPTCHA Naturally, cyber criminals have found ways to imitate these familiar security checks and turn them into tools for deception. One dangerous example is a scam known as ClickFix . It tricks people into running harmful instructions on their own computers. Instead of directly breaking through a computer’s security protections, attackers persuade you to perform the dangerous action – making it appear to be part of a legitimate security procedure. How ClickFix works Imagine you’re shopping online or creating a new account. You visit what appears to be an ordinary website, perhaps through a search result. The website may look genuine. In fact, it’s likely a legitimate site the cyber criminals have secretly compromised. As you browse, a familiar verification screen appears, asking you to confirm you are human. You click the checkbox, expecting to continue browsing. But something unusual happens. Instead of completing the verification, the page displays additional instructions . Example of a fake CAPTCHA asking a user to paste a command into Windows ‘Run command’ tool. UOregon Information Security Office First, it secretly puts a computer command in your clipboard, the temporary storage area for copied text before you paste it. Then, it asks you to press a keyboard shortcut, such as Windows+R, that opens a dialog box on your computer, and to paste the command in there. This can happen on any computer – on Windows it will be a tool called Run command, while on Apple it will be Terminal. These are legitimate tools for advanced users, but here they’re weaponised to install malware. In Australia, the national cyber security agency found a ClickFix campaign that’s spreading malware called Vidar Stealer . It can steal passwords, browsing information and other sensitive data. The threat is global . Criminals may use information stolen via malware to access personal accounts, steal money or launch further cyber attacks. The CAPTCHA box to prove you’re not a robot could be a scam. Here’s how to spot it. How do I stay safe? A genuine CAPTCHA will never ask you to copy-paste text or run computer commands. ClickFix is effective because it exploits a familiar habit. We’ve become accustomed to following verification instructions online. Importantly, simply clicking the fake CAPTCHA doesn’t necessarily infect your computer. The critical step occurs when you follow the additional instructions and execute the malicious command. To avoid falling prey to such scams, keep these tips in mind. Don’t follow instructions you don’t understand. Never run a computer command simply because a website asks you to prove you’re human. If a CAPTCHA behaves differently from what you’d normally expect, stop and question it. Don’t download unknown programs. Be cautious if a website unexpectedly asks you to fix a technical problem, install software or change your computer’s security settings. Only download software from trusted sources, such as official vendor websites or approved app stores. Keep everything up to date. Regular updates to your computer, browser and security software help protect against known security weaknesses, although they can’t guarantee protection against every new attack. Stay on top of your passwords. Use strong, unique passwords or passphrases and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible. Browse carefully. When accessing banking or other sensitive services, use a trusted bookmark or type the website address directly rather than following unexpected links. However, remember that even legitimate websites can sometimes be compromised. I think I made a mistake, now what? If you accidentally click a suspicious CAPTCHA, stop immediately. Don’t copy and paste anything. If you’ve already executed an unfamiliar command, disconnect your device from the internet and seek technical assistance. For a work computer, contact the IT team. You should also use another trusted device to change potentially exposed passwords and check all important accounts for suspicious activity. The next time a website asks you to prove you’re human, remember the check happens in your browser. If it asks you to reach into your computer, it isn’t checking you. It’s using you. articles.content: Yingqi Zhang excavates in the fossil chamber of Baxian Cave in China. Kira Westaway , CC BY-NC Our distant relative, Homo erectus , is known for many human achievements. It was the first human to exit Africa and the first to use fire. It also survived for almost two million years in open woodland savannahs. But flexible, adaptive and mobile are not usually words to describe this ancient human. Until now. Two new papers published today in Nature by our international team of researchers paint these humans in a very different light. The team explored two neighbouring caves in Guangxi province of southern China . They uncovered nine human teeth that contain many secrets about how these ancient humans survived. The landscape around the entrance to Baxian cave in China. Yingqi Zhang , CC BY-NC A late survivor Eight of the teeth were identified as Homo erectus using their shape and ancient genetic signatures. Their age revealed this species was still surviving in southern China between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. This is 100–200,000 years later than previously established. At that time Homo erectus was thought to have disappeared from China . This new timeline was established using a combination of five different dating techniques. These were applied to the teeth, surrounding cave sediments and mineral formations. The results confidently place these humans in this landscape at a time when we thought they were already regionally extinct. This is the youngest securely dated evidence for Homo erectus in mainland China. At home in the rainforest Rainforests are demanding environments. It can be difficult to find food, move through the dense landscape and survive. In fact, the spread of rainforests in Southeast Asia has been linked to the disappearance of some ancient human groups. The teeth were discovered in cave sediments with over 19,000 other animal fossils. Their chemical signatures suggest the people they belonged to were living in dense rainforest conditions. The signatures for the Homo erectus teeth also showed they were drinking and eating in this challenging environment – a far cry from the “less demanding” open woodland savannahs. Scientists thought only our own species, Homo sapiens could cope with dense rainforests . But the new evidence from southern China shows the relationship between ancient humans and tropical forests was more complex. Could it be that the younger populations of Homo erectus were more flexible and adaptable than we previously considered? The nine human teeth found in Naxian and Baxian Caves – eight of which have been confidently identified as Homo erectus . Kira Westaway , CC BY-NC Travelling far as children Additional chemical signatures from the Homo erectus teeth were used to reconstruct how they moved across the landscape. Strontium is a chemical signal in the enamel that is linked to the local geology. By analysing the strontium in these teeth, we found that some individuals may have spent their childhoods moving through the wider forested regions. The humans may have covered surprisingly large areas rather than remaining in one small, localised area around the caves. They may have travelled as far as northern Vietnam and mainland Southeast Asia. Our understanding of this mobility is restricted to just their childhoods. This is because the strontium signature is only laid down in the enamel during the first seven years of life. Illustration of Homo erectus lurking in the shadows of the tropical forest in Guangxi. Garciart/Joannes-Boyau , CC BY-NC This means our awareness of their adult movement is limited. The proximity of the caves and the overlap in timelines suggest a single population of Homo erectus was surviving within at least a roughly 15 kilometre radius in the rainforests between 324,000 an 184,000 years ago. Rather than being restricted to their preferred open landscapes, these populations had the ability to survive in tropical forests. Furthermore, they could move across a wider landscape outside the limestone hills. The big picture This newly discovered ability has implications for our understanding of the fate of Homo erectus in China and calls for a reassessment of their flexibility and adaptation to environments outside their preferred habitat. It also questions our assumptions over the fate of Homo erectus in Java and the cause of their ultimate extinction. It was assumed they were unable to adapt when their preferred open woodland environment changed to rainforest. But this new evidence in China suggests they may have had the ability to be more flexible in Java. If so, what was the environmental event that caused their downfall if not pressure from the encroaching rainforests? This can only be solved by the use of a similar chemical signature analysis of human and animal teeth in other regions, as seen in these two studies. One thing is clear: the skills and abilities thought to be the traits of only modern humans are increasingly being observed in ancient humans. Further analysis of fossil human teeth may provide more secrets. Kira Westaway receives funding from The Australian Research Council. articles.content: Jean-Claude Stahl/Te Papa , CC BY-NC-ND The last bird to go extinct in Aotearoa New Zealand was a tiny wren that disappeared from a small island off the southern tip of Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972. Stead’s bush wren , or mātuhituhi, was the last of its kind. The North and South Island bush wrens had already gone extinct by 1955 and 1968, respectively. Stead’s bush wren followed after ship rats invaded its last stronghold on Taukihepa Big South Cape Island. This incursion also caused the extinction of the tutukiwi Stewart Island snipe and greater short-tailed bat , as well as the near-extinction of the South Island tīeke saddleback . Mātuhituhi bush wrens were tiny forest specialists. Paul Martinson/Te Papa Tongarewa Museum of New Zealand , CC BY-NC-ND The rats were likely introduced accidentally from fishing boats around 1963 and exterminated the wrens rapidly within a few years. Six birds were moved to nearby Kaimohu Island in 1964, but despite the best efforts to save them, the last two individuals were seen in 1972. The extinction of Stead’s bush wren shows how vulnerable small ground-dwelling birds are . But scientists know surprisingly little about them . Now, our new study based on ancient DNA reveals the evolutionary and ecological history of these lost birds as well as a previously unrecognised member of the bush wren family. Deep and dynamic evolutionary history Bush wrens ( Xenicus longipes ) were once widespread across New Zealand, with different subspecies on the North, South and Stewart Island. The historical and fossil record shows they were a forest specialist with limited dispersal ability. Bush wrens belong to New Zealand’s unique wren family (acanthisittidae) that also includes the living pīwauwau rock wren and tītipounamu rifleman as well as four other recently extinct species . New Zealand wrens are representatives of an ancient lineage which diverged from all other song birds (passerines) about 70 million years ago . Our analysis of ancient DNA from specimens held in museum collections worldwide shows bush wrens evolved about six million years ago when the uplift of the Southern Alps created a variety of new habitats. The North ( Xenicus stokesii ) and South Island ( Xenicus longipes ) bush wren diverged about 2.6 million years ago. Back then, the southern end of the North Island was connected to the South Island and as marine straits in the Manawatu region narrowed, bush wrens could island hop from south to north. Our analyses strongly suggest they should be recognised as distinct species rather than subspecies. South Island bush wrens remained stable until about 500,000 years ago when we identified a near simultaneous, major diversification event that split them into northern, central and southern lineages. Stead’s bush wren emerged about 94,000 years ago. A new member of the bush wren family The key to disentangling the evolutionary history of bush wrens was our ability to use ancient DNA to genetically sex specimens and to re-examine the plumage of male and female museum specimens. Prior to this, scientists were convinced there were no plumage differences between the sexes. We found that different bush wren lineages do in fact show marked plumage differences between sexes, with the exception of the South Island bush wren from Fiordland, where males and females both had green plumage. When we put all the genetic and plumage data together, we found a new bush wren hiding in plain sight within the central and northern South Island. It was different to all the other recognised bush wrens. We named this new subspecies the Tōtaranui bush wren ( Xenicus longipes perditus ) after the Māori name for Queen Charlotte Sound. In its Latin name, perditus stands for lost. Genetic sexing was key to unravelling the highly variable plumage of bush wrens. These museum specimens show North Island bush wren juvenile (A) and male (B); Tōtaranui bush wren female (C) and male (D); Fiordland bush wren female (E) and male (F) and Stead’s bush wren female (G) and male (H). Jean-Claude Stahl/Te Papa , CC BY-NC-ND Ice Age climate change What caused this near simultaneous burst of diversification in bush wrens? Some 2.58 million years ago, the world entered an Ice Age and cycled through 19 to 20 shifts between cold glacial and warm interglacial periods. Forests and the animals that lived in them retreated into separate areas during cold periods and expanded across the South Island when it warmed . Initially, these cycles were relatively mild, lasting around 40,000 years. However, when Earth’s wobble on its axis shifted around one millions years ago, these cycles intensified and extended, lasting about 100,000 years. While bush wrens could buffer climatic changes to an extent, they eventually reached a tipping point and retreated to multiple different refugia . Their diversification is a prime example of glacier-driven evolution . The extinction of the Stead’s bush wren marked a turning point for New Zealand conservation and the management of rodents on islands. Yet bush wrens continue to provide lessons for future ecosystem restoration and conservation management, especially for species with strict habitat requirements. Accelerating human-driven environmental impacts and climate change will put ecosystems under increased pressure and exacerbate the impacts of invasive species and habitat modification. It is imperative we do what we can now to preserve genetic diversity within threatened species and increase the climate resilience of ecosystems before it is too late. articles.content: Chiociolla/Getty Images Have you ever sprayed a perfume in a department store on a paper strip and loved the smell, but it didn’t perform the same when you sprayed it on your skin? It’s a common experience. It all has to do with how the molecules in the perfume evaporate and interact with your skin. That chemistry also explains why the same perfume may smell amazing on you, but on someone else it can smell completely different, and sometimes not nearly as pleasant. That’s because each of us has different “skin chemistry”. As a result, perfumes will behave differently, and the smell our noses detect will vary. To understand why and how this happens, first we need to look at what is a perfume, chemically speaking. What’s in a perfume? Simply put, a perfume is a mixture of various fragrance molecules, typically dissolved in alcohol. Perfumers carefully combine these ingredients into what are known as “top”, “middle” and “base” notes. Top notes, such as citrus compounds like limonene, are highly volatile, will evaporate quickly, and not stay on the skin for long. Middle notes, often floral or fruity molecules, emerge after the top notes fade because they’re less volatile and stick around for longer. Base notes, including musks, woods and resins, are the heaviest or largest molecules, so they evaporate more slowly and will linger the longest. When a perfume is sprayed onto paper, the fragrance molecules evaporate (change from liquid to gas) in a relatively predictable way. Their ability to escape into the air is mainly determined by intermolecular forces – interactions between molecules. The stronger those forces are, the harder it is for a molecule to break away and change from liquid to gas. Molecule size and shape also play a role here. So, the top notes evaporate first because they’re small and have weak intermolecular forces, while base notes are the opposite. Knowing all this about the molecules is what lets perfumers create fragrances that will release their notes fairly predictably. But it gets more complicated once fragrance hits the skin. Perfumes are formulated to evaporate in a predictable way, but there are many factors that can affect how the molecules behave. Jay Huang/Unsplash How skin chemistry enters the picture While a paper tester strip is a fairly neutral surface, we have various molecules on the skin. These interact with the perfume and can not only change the order of the molecules being released, but also alter or mask the resulting scent. The main skin factors that will influence the scent of perfume are: moisture content and oiliness temperature pH level microbiome. Moisture and oiliness Hydration is one of the main factors. Dry skin tends to absorb heavier or larger fragrance molecules more readily, while moist or oily skin provides a better surface for fragrance molecules to sit on and evaporate gradually. This often improves how long the perfume lasts and its projection – how much others around you can smell it. This is why the same perfume could last all day on one person, but only for a couple of hours on another. Temperature Warmer skin increases evaporation, causing perfumes to develop more quickly and sometimes smell stronger. A person with naturally warmer skin may experience top notes disappearing much faster. Base notes may become noticeable within minutes rather than an hour. This can make it seem as though the perfume “skips” the top notes. pH level The natural acidity of the skin, often referred to as skin pH, may also subtly influence fragrance performance. Human skin is slightly acidic, typically around pH 4.5 to 5.5. While most fragrance ingredients remain stable within this range, subtle pH changes could cause fragrance ingredients to react differently . As a result some floral notes may weaken, some musks may become more prominent, some citrus notes may smell sharper or disappear rapidly. Skin microbiome Perhaps the most fascinating factor is our skin microbiome . Our skin is home to billions of microorganisms , including bacteria and fungi. These microbes interact with compounds found in sweat and skin oils, producing volatile organic compounds that contribute to each person’s unique scent profile . The microbes can also metabolise fragrance molecules. This can produce new odours, enhance some notes, or suppress others. It’s another reason why a fragrance could smell wonderful on one person and unpleasant on another. Always test perfume on your skin, not just on a paper strip. Gabrijelagal/Getty Images Perfumes can be fickle All this means that when you apply a perfume, it’s not interacting with a neutral surface, like a piece of paper. It’s combining with your own unique chemical background. A floral fragrance that smells fresh and rosy on one person may seem sharper, sweeter or even slightly sour on another, because it’s blending with different molecules on that person’s skin. Even the same perfume on the same person can smell slightly different from one day to the next. Changes in hydration, hormone levels, diet (spicy or garlicky foods can make you smell differently), ambient temperature and skin condition can all affect fragrance performance. It pays to keep all this in mind when buying and using fragrances. First, never judge a fragrance solely on a paper test strip. They’re good for a first impression, but can’t predict how a perfume will behave on your skin. Always test a fragrance on your wrist and wear it for several hours before deciding whether to buy it. Second, don’t be disappointed if a perfume smells different on you than on paper or on your friend’s wrist. Biologically we’re all unique and you might have better luck with a different fragrance. Finally, if you want a fragrance to last longer, applying an unscented lotion before spraying can often help – it will make the perfume evaporate slower. articles.content: Not too long ago, when politicians wanted to reach the public they had to get past journalists, editors and producers, who collectively decided what made the news. But now, politicians can post, livestream, and message voters directly on social media platforms. On platforms such as Instagram, Tiktok and YouTube, engagement algorithms designed to hold viewers’ attention determine what voters see and how often. The shift to algorithmic social media has been great for populist politicians around the world, who position themselves as representing the “will of the people”. In our recent research (under peer review), we collected 35,500 public posts from TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, posted during elections by parties and politicians across the political spectrum in several countries. Based on our analysis of this data, we found the “social media playbook” shared by many populist parties has four basic moves: build an audience provoke the audience encourage the audience to spread the message listen to the audience and give them more of what they want. These moves use the rules of social media platforms to gain attention, support and votes. What is populism? Populism is a word that gets thrown around a lot , and is often used as a euphemism for the far right . On a more careful view, the defining feature of populism is it splits society into “the pure people” and “the corrupt elite”. It holds that politics should express the “general will” of the people. Populism is a thin ideology that can come from the left or the right. It can be combined with fuller ideologies from nationalism to socialism. Social media fits well with populism , as it gives populists a channel to invoke the support of people against the establishment . Platform populists around the world Populists across the globe have made the most of social media. In Argentina, the rise of Javier Milei to presidency in 2023 is partly attributed to his TikTok account of 1.5 million followers . In Germany, two populist parties, both with a highly visible TikTok presence, doubled their vote at the 2025 election. In New York, Zohran Mamdani rose from 1% in early polls to mayor in 2025 , helped by short videos on TikTok and Instagram . In the United Kingdom, Nigel Farage entered Parliament in 2024 with more than 800,000 highly engaged TikTok followers . And in Australia, One Nation, dismissed for decades as a fringe party , has polled 24-31% on primary votes this year. Its rise has been accompanied by cartoons and AI-generated ads with millions of views on social media. These parties and leaders differ sharply in politics, but their methods are remarkably alike. The social media playbook Our research found a social media playbook of four moves: build, provoke, spread, listen. The first move is to “build” audiences across several platforms, using free accounts, follower networks and livestreaming. The leader is the brand, and short-form videos filmed with front-facing cameras project apparent authenticity. Building may also involve values-based content that makes the party seem reasonable and relatable. The second move is to “provoke” by simplifying issues, finding people to blame, and getting headlines. Short posts in simple language will make bold claims about complex problems such as housing or cost of living. Often the “corrupt elite”, the media or outsiders are blamed. Part of the goal here is to push the stories from social media into mainstream news . The third move is to “spread” the message via followers. Share buttons, comment threads and tools such as TikTok’s duet and stitch make every follower a potential broadcaster. The platform’s engagement algorithms will then push the message to new audiences. Finally, “listen” uses audience engagement as live opinion polling. Platform analytics show which posts land within minutes, and ad tools can test different versions of a message. Whatever draws the most reactions becomes the next message, or even the next policy. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a big part of the playbook. The platform engagement algorithms are a kind of AI, and generative AI tools for producing text, images and video make all the moves cheaper and faster. A single video can be cut, captioned and translated for diverse demographics, and millions of likes, comments, views sorted by mood for targeted campaigns in minutes. An adversary can be made vivid with a synthetic image, as One Nation’s AI-made Victorian election ad shows . AI agents can even run accounts that post, reply and share around the clock, making a few supporters look like many. What we can do Mainstream parties struggle with copying these moves because complex policies don’t fit into 15-second clips, and sound scripted beside a leader talking straight to the camera. Also, parties chasing broad support may avoid sharp messages that rally one group but alienate another. Platforms profit from this populist playbook, as their algorithms amplify the kind of messaging that keeps people scrolling and drives advertising revenue. Attempts to make platforms offer a simpler, chronological feed of posts – such as the Australian government’s “My Feed, My Way” bill – would weaken part of this approach, but most of it would still work. That is why media literacy matters now and into the future, especially as AI blurs what’s real. This populist approach works by getting people to play along. So next time you see a post that makes you angry or hands you a villain, pause for a moment. Ask who made it, why, and what has been left out. You might have to look up some other credible sources on the topic – not just asking a chatbot – and gain a broader knowledge. Engagement algorithms are trained on our reactions. The most effective thing you can do is to stop and think before you hit share. The platform engagement algorithms are a kind of AI, and generative AI tools for producing text, images and video make all the moves cheaper and faster. A single video can be cut, captioned and translated for diverse demographics, and millions of likes, comments, views sorted by mood for targeted campaigns in minutes. An adversary can be made vivid with a synthetic image, as One Nation’s AI-made Victorian election ad shows . AI agents can even run accounts that post, reply and share around the clock, making a few supporters look like many. What we can do Mainstream parties struggle with copying these moves because complex policies don’t fit into 15-second clips, and sound scripted beside a leader talking straight to the camera. Also, parties chasing broad support may avoid sharp messages that rally one group but alienate another. Platforms profit from this populist playbook, as their algorithms amplify the kind of messaging that keeps people scrolling and drives advertising revenue. Attempts to make platforms offer a simpler, chronological feed of posts – such as the Australian government’s “My Feed, My Way” bill – would weaken part of this approach, but most of it would still work. That is why media literacy matters now and into the future, especially as AI blurs what’s real. This populist approach works by getting people to play along. So next time you see a post that makes you angry or hands you a villain, pause for a moment. Ask who made it, why, and what has been left out. You might have to look up some other credible sources on the topic – not just asking a chatbot – and gain a broader knowledge. Engagement algorithms are trained on our reactions. The most effective thing you can do is to stop and think before you hit share.
