articles.content: Chen Liji/Getty Australian Aboriginal people have seen the sky as an integral part of their world for at least 65,000 years. The Aboriginal sky is a world that reflects our Earth-bound world, so understanding the sky is an important part of understanding our place here on Earth. As a result, Aboriginal songs, stories and art show evidence of thousands of years of studying and understanding the sky. And in the ancient Aboriginal traditions, we see the traces of giant intellectual achievements. The stars and the planets In the clear black skies that predated streetlights and satellites, Aboriginal elders would look up at the sky night after night. They would see how all the stars rotate around us as if embedded in a crystal sphere, each night giving us a slightly different view. And they realised that not all stars are the same. While Western astronomers preached that the stars were constant in brightness, Aboriginal astronomers noticed that some, such as the famous Betelgeuse in Orion’s shoulder (in Western tradition) or at the front of his canoe (in Yolngu tradition, in Arnhem Land) brighten and dim over time . The Western Constellation of Orion is seen as the Djulpan constellation by the Yolngu people. The three bright stars of Orion’s belt are three brothers fishing in their canoe, having illegally caight a kingfish, represented by the Orion Nebula, or Orion’s sword in the western tradition. The bow of the canoe, at the bottom, is the star Betelgeuse, whose variability was noted by Aboriginal astronomers. drawn by author , CC BY Against that backdrop, Aboriginal astronomers saw the planets moving amongst the stars. They saw how most planets appear to move steadily along a path that modern astronomers call the ecliptic, and Wardaman people from the Northern Territory called “ Yondorrin ”. They understood how Mars would sometimes pause its steady travel across the sky, and backtrack a few steps, before resuming its forward march. They understood how Venus , as the Morning Star, always rose just before dawn, or as the Evening Star set just after sunset, but never appeared high in the night sky. . Modern astronomers explain these movements in terms of planetary orbits. But the ancient Aboriginal astronomers fitted them into their own cultural framework, with stories of creator spirits, their stories always staying true to their careful observational data. In Yolngu tradition, Venus, or Barnumbirr, never rises high in the sky because of the string that her sisters tied to her. We now see this string as ‘zodiacal light’, caused by sunlight reflecting off dust in the solar system. Ray Norris , CC BY Lunar and solar eclipses A solar eclipse, that rare spine-chilling apparition when the Sun goes dark during the daytime, is caused by the Moon passing in front of the Sun. Some Aboriginal groups had figured this out too, and explained it as the Moon-man covering the Sun-woman as they made love. The Aboriginal astronomers passed this knowledge on across the generations, even though only about one in ten generations would actually witness a solar eclipse. On the other hand, a lunar eclipse, when the Moon goes blood red at night, is caused by Earth blocking the sunlight that normally lights up the Moon. This happens when the Sun and Moon are on exactly opposite sides of the sky, which is not at all obvious to the untrained eye. What Aboriginal genius had that flash of insight, while watching a lunar eclipse, that this eclipse was caused by the precise juxtaposition of the Sun and Moon on opposite sides of the sky? That realisation was an important intellectual leap, and we won’t ever know the name of the ancient astronomer who first realised it. But we still see traces in the Aboriginal cultural legacy. The movement of the tides We are all familiar with the rise and fall of the tides on the beach. But their cause eluded astronomers for years. Galileo failed to explain them, coming up with an entirely incorrect explanation which denied the Moon any role . In contrast, ancient Yolngu astronomers recognised the tides were caused by the Moon, and realised that you can predict the height of the tide from the phase of the Moon . Unfortunately we have no way of dating this knowledge. But given that other Aboriginal astronomical traditions stretch back many hundreds or thousands of years , it is likely that this Yolngu knowledge is far older than our modern Western understanding. This enabled Yolngu people to safely navigate the crocodile-infested waters of the Arafura Sea, where Galileo surely would have perished. So this understanding of the sky went beyond simply understanding how the sky worked. It also had practical applications, enabling ancient Aboriginal people to navigate across and around Australia, and build sophisticated calendars which would help them manage the land and their food supply. Bringing different knowledges together This ancient astronomical knowledge fits into the growing appreciation of the vast body of Aboriginal achievements in navigation, medicine and agriculture . By comparing modern science with Aboriginal culture, we can clearly see the depth and intellectual power of ancient Aboriginal cultures. This article itself, as well as our other work , is the result of bringing different knowledges together. One of us (Ray) has spent a lifetime studying the sky through astrophysics. The other (Bruce) observes the sky through Aboriginal eyes, and has learnt from traditional stories and paintings passed on by other Aboriginal people. When science meets Aboriginal culture, we enrich our understanding of both. articles.content: Bill Henske/ARCUS , CC BY-SA The usual advice for people visiting wilderness areas is to leave nothing but footprints. But as our new study shows, even footprints may disturb rare ecosystems in Antarctica and cause irreversible changes. Antarctica harbours some of the world’s rarest and most precious ecosystems, including the permafrost soils of the vast, ice-free McMurdo Dry Valleys – one of the driest deserts on Earth. Despite the harsh conditions, the ice-cemented soil layers are home to unique, localised microbial communities and tiny spineless creatures such as nematodes, tardigrades and rotifers that survive in thin water films around grains of sand. Environmental protection is a key focus of Antarctic governance and quarantine and decontamination protocols prescribe comprehensive inspection and cleaning of footwear and other field gear prior to departure to the continent. But such protocols are in place to primarily prevent people from bringing and spreading new invasive species in Antarctica. Our study focused on the possibility of people redistributing local microbial communities between sites and unwittingly disturbing fragile ecosystems. Disrupting locally adapted ecosystems While the number of established non-native species in Antarctica is low compared with most continents, biological invasions are on the rise . At least a dozen non-native land invertebrates, including soil-dwelling springtails and mites, and several plant species have been recorded south of 60°S, particularly near research stations and heavily visited areas. Human activity – including scientific operations, logistics and tourism – is the primary route of invasion for non-native species. Once introduced, climate warming is expected to increase the chances these species will survive Antarctic conditions and spread. But for now, perhaps the biggest threat is intra-continental transfer. This is when endemic Antarctic species that are already locally adapted spread beyond their usual distribution ranges. The most likely candidates for this kind of spread are microbes, which play a fundamental role in ecosystems as primary producers and nutrient cyclers. The extreme conditions of Antarctic soils mean that even common and globally distributed bacterial lineages have to adapt to the point that they evolve into strains found nowhere else on Earth. Within the Dry Valleys, communities are so specific that each valley has a unique microbial signature . Microbial DNA tracks movement between valleys Our study asked whether people transfer microbes between valleys and potentially disrupt local assemblages. We compared microbial species identified in local soil with those found on surfaces of field equipment, helicopter skids and boots. In one analysis, we found that 73% of swabbed footwear harboured DNA from microbes we also detected at upstream locations in a single day of operational movements. While cleaning and disinfection changed the microbial communities present on field equipment, we found this did not completely eliminate the transfer of microbial taxa between gear and local soils. Field operations in the Dry Valleys are therefore likely contributing to the movement of locally adapted and valley-specific microbial communities. We haven’t yet determined the potential ecological impact of our findings. But these results clearly emphasise the importance of biosecurity monitoring and decontamination protocols across Antarctic field programmes. New Zealanders have accepted the need to disinfect boots to prevent the spread of pathogens such as kauri dieback disease. In Antarctica’s Dry Valleys, we need to strengthen contamination protocols to disinfect boots and field gear if more than one site is visited, while also upping biosecurity monitoring for microbes and other easily dispersed species. Angela (Ang) McGaughran receives funding from the Royal Society Te Apārangi and received proof-of-concept funding from Antarctica New Zealand for the microbial study.

articles.content: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images If you’re like me, when you pick up a compass you can’t help but spin it this way and that, to see if you can trick it. It’s hard to resist experimenting with a spooky force we can’t see or feel ourselves. Yet it always turns the compass needle back towards north. Even in today’s high-tech world, compasses are useful navigation tools. A compass works without power, unlike GPS, and in any weather and lighting conditions, as opposed to navigation using the Sun, stars or landmarks. If you know which way north is, you can determine any direction. Like all cool phenomena, the explanation of how a compass works is not magic – it’s physics. And people have been making use of this particular aspect of physics for more than 2,000 years . A lodestone spoon The earliest versions of the compass were developed in ancient China. They were spoon-shaped and made of lodestones , pieces of the naturally magnetic mineral magnetite. When allowed to rotate freely, the spoon handle would align itself with a particular direction (north–south). This was used to organise and harmonise environments, as part of a practice you might know as feng shui . Model of a Han dynasty (206 BC–220 AD) south-indicating ladle. Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-NC-SA At the time, it was known that some materials were naturally magnetic – able to attract one another. However, it wasn’t clear exactly what was causing a compass to align itself north–south until 1600, when English physicist William Gilbert deduced that Earth itself acted as a giant magnet . An invisible field Like all magnets, Earth generates a magnetic field – an invisible region within which its magnetic forces act. Electricity and magnetism are closely connected. Together, they form one of the fundamental interactions in physics: electromagnetism . Magnetic fields can be created by electric currents, which are the movements of charged particles; a changing magnetic field can also induce an electrical current. Our planet spins around an axis once roughly every 24 hours, which is why we have a night and day cycle . The end points of this axis are the North Pole and the South Pole. Beneath Earth’s surface, in the outer core, electrically conducting liquid metals circulate in convective currents . This movement generates electrical currents. Paired with Earth’s rotation around its axis, these currents maintain a global-scale magnetic field . It extends out into space like a giant, invisible bubble, known as the magnetosphere. And it’s this global-scale magnetic field that allows a compass to work. Earth’s magnetic field is called the magnetosphere. NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio In modern compasses, a magnetised metal needle has replaced the lodestone spoon. That needle is mounted on a low-friction pivot so it has minimal resistance to the effects of external magnetic fields. As a result, unless there’s a magnet directly nearby, the needle will align itself with Earth’s magnetic north–south direction. If you’ve ever found that a compass needle didn’t perfectly align with north–south, it might be because it detected a localised magnetic field. Electrical devices such as your phone produce weak magnetic fields. These can affect a compass, causing it to deviate from Earth’s magnetic field. Watch what happens when a magnet is placed next to a compass. Which way does a compass really point? All magnets have two opposite points – a “north” pole and a “south” pole. If you have two magnets, opposite poles (north–south) will pull towards each other, while the same poles (south–south or north–north) will push away. The next bit will seem a little confusing, but it’s key to understand why compasses point towards the geographic north. Because opposites attract, the “north” arrow on a compass points towards the “south” pole of Earth’s global-scale magnetic field – the area where field lines point down into Earth’s surface. Despite it having a magnetic polarity of “south”, we call this spot the north magnetic pole because it’s located close to the geographic North Pole in the Arctic. Earth also has a magnetic south pole, and you guessed it – it’s located near the South Pole in Antarctica, while being the “north” counterpart of Earth’s magnetic field. Why compasses point towards the north. Useful in more ways than one The magnetic poles don’t align perfectly with the poles of Earth’s rotational axis. The reason for this is that Earth’s magnetic field is dynamic. The ever-changing motion of liquid metal in Earth’s outer core means the global magnetic field changes, too. In fact, the magnetic north and south poles slowly change their locations, and the entire magnetic field has even flipped its polarity in the past, making the two switch places. Earth’s magnetic field also acts as a protective barrier from space weather generated by our Sun: there’s a constant stream of charged particles coming our way, known as solar wind. The global magnetic field helps to shield Earth and our atmosphere. Mars, by contrast, no longer has a strong global-scale magnetic field to act as a protective shield. Interactions with solar wind have, over time, contributed to the loss of much of Mars’ atmosphere . So, the same invisible magnetic field that turns a compass needle also plays a much bigger role in helping to keep Earth our home . articles.content: Rob Hampson/Unsplash You search online for a new pair of running shoes. Later, while scrolling through Instagram, an ad appears for the very shoes you were considering. Perhaps you watched a video about travelling to Japan, and now your Facebook feed is full of flight deals and hotel offers. The timing can feel uncanny. Some people even wonder whether their phones are listening to private conversations . But advertising platforms don’t need to listen to know what might interest us. Our searches, clicks, purchases and other online activities can reveal far more than we realise. Australia’s digital duty of care bill , which is currently under Senate inquiry , would require online services to take steps to protect users from serious online harms. As part of this, the government introduced the My Feed, My Way initiative . It would give Australians the option to choose social media feeds that only show content from users they follow, as opposed to a feed full of algorithmically recommended content. However, these proposed controls don’t necessarily affect the advertisements appearing in the feeds. So even if we gain greater control over our social media feeds, what about the ads? You can control ads – to an extent Facebook and Instagram already allow users to influence the advertisements they see. Through Meta’s Accounts Centre , users can manage advertising preferences, select topics they want to see fewer advertisements about, and hide ads from particular advertisers. But this doesn’t guarantee the ads will completely disappear. On YouTube, Google’s My Ad Centre allows users to manage advertising topics, limit certain sensitive categories (such as gambling or alcohol) and turn off personalised advertising. TikTok also provides advertising controls , including options to manage advertising topics, mute advertisers and review activity shared by advertising partners. These settings provide useful choices, but there is an important limitation. Changing the ads you see doesn’t necessarily change what information a platform collects about you. For example, selecting fewer fitness advertisements on Instagram doesn’t prevent Meta from receiving information about your visits to fitness websites. To understand why, we need to look at where advertising information comes from. How do platforms know what interests us? Online platforms that serve ads collect information about our online activities, both within their apps and from other websites. Businesses may use tracking technologies, such as the Meta Pixel , to share information about your visit with Meta. It’s essentially a trail of data you create while browsing the internet. That information can help advertisers reach people who’ve previously shown interest in their products, and deliver targeted ads to them. Platforms also use our in-app activities to predict our interests and personalise ads. This can make advertisements appear remarkably accurate – to the point where you might think they’re actually listening to you. In June , Meta announced it was expanding how it uses information shared by other businesses. Previously used to personalise ads, this data will now also help to personalise feeds and AI responses: We already use this data – like games you play or purchases you make on other websites – to make the ads you see more relevant. In the future, we’ll use this information to personalise other parts of your experience. Meta also announced users will be able to control whether its platforms can use this data to personalise the content they’re served. But there’s a distinction between restricting how information is used and preventing businesses from collecting and passing it on in the first place. What does Australian law say? Australia already has privacy laws that apply to targeted advertising. Under the current privacy act , organisations covered by the Australian Privacy Principles must comply with requirements governing the use and disclosure of personal information for direct marketing. These include circumstances in which individuals can request that their personal information no longer be used or disclosed for direct marketing. However, these protections are not equivalent to a universal ban on online tracking or personalised advertising. The proposed digital duty of care legislation primarily addresses online safety and user empowerment. Its provisions for controlling our feeds don’t explicitly establish a right to disable targeted advertising. However, the government is also currently revising our privacy laws. The draft bill proposes a “fair and reasonable” test for collecting, using and disclosing personal information. articles.content: IDREES MOHAMMED/Getty When a massive outage hit Microsoft late last week, much of the digital world ground to a halt. The outage wiped out key Microsoft services including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, which are used by more than 430 million people around the world . As email and internal communications froze, the operations of governments and businesses went dark alongside them, triggering an economic paralysis that could cost billions of dollars . While the global economy absorbs the brunt of this paralysis, Microsoft faces both a severe reputational hit and contractual penalties that could reach up to US$800 million per day for services they failed to deliver. Such a catastrophic outage shows just how precarious our modern digital infrastructure is. It depends on a handful of big tech companies, which have essentially become too big to fail. So how did we end up in this situation? And is there a way out? Digital dependency The initial source of Microsoft’s failure was incredibly innocuous. Data centres usually share the load of user demands across systems all over the world. However, last week, a small configuration change caused the company to lose control of some of their computers . Unable to share the load, these computers dropped user requests onto other systems, overwhelming them and producing more outages. This pattern repeated over and over again until the company lost almost complete control of their network. Worse, disconnected user devices – phones, email clients and business systems – all automatically tried to reconnect at once, crashing Microsoft’s systems all over again . Historically, a tech outage might affect a single company. But the reason Microsoft’s outage could impact millions of people comes down to a business revolution that silently took place over 20 years ago . Software was once something that was sold to companies once for an upfront cost. In this model, purchasers held great power – only buying new versions if the update justified the expense. Yet, these upfront expenses also scared consumers off. Drawing inspiration from telecommunications, gyms and real estate leasing, the tech industry transitioned to renting access to their products, creating what is now known as “ software as a service ”. In theory, everyone profited from this model . Software vendors could bank more reliable cash flow, and customers could transition to regular smaller payments, rather than stumping up for large upfront costs. Ultimately, this change shifted the balance of power towards tech companies. Instead of purchasing features they needed, consumers handed the keys to their operational kingdoms to the “software as service” providers, and locked themselves into highly expensive long-term contracts in the process. Too big to fail The global financial crisis in 2008 introduced the world to the idea of too big to fail. When it hit, the public was left to pick up the pieces of banks that had become too systemically important to be allowed to fail. Unfortunately, it appears we haven’t really learned those lessons. Instead, we’ve spent the last few years living through a slow-motion version of that with the tech industry. Centralisation, consolidation and unchecked monopolies have left our digital lives, our businesses and our governments in an incredibly precarious place. On one level or another, almost everything on the internet goes through Google , Microsoft, Meta , Amazon Web Services or CrowdStrike – all of which have had major outages over recent years. These big tech giants earned our trust by providing unified, seemingly invincible infrastructure. But the convenience that comes with centralisation holds a trap. Unlike the banking sector in 2008, when these tech titans fail, they don’t need to ask governments to bail them out. Instead, their centrality forces the entire digital economy to bear the costs of their outage. Developing digital sovereignty Escaping the reliance on a few tech giants for our national infrastructure, businesses and citizens’ data has spurned the push for so-called digital sovereignty . Europe is leading the way on this . By actively funding decentralised cloud infrastructure and homegrown software, governments are ensuring that an American tech failure cannot knock out a local hospital. The world must adopt a similar blueprint. Australia, in particular, is well placed to grasp the opportunities that digital sovereignty brings. We already have the raw engineering talent. Companies such as Atlassian, Apromore, Airwallex and Canva have proven we can build world-class digital tools. If governments strategically invested in local tech ecosystems, they wouldn’t just be buying digital insurance. They would drive much-needed market competition, dilute the power of big-tech monopolies and spread out systemic risks – ensuring that a single point of failure could never bring the economy to its knees. This is not to say we should divest ourselves of any connection to big-tech platforms, which do and will continue to provide useful services. But if our entire global economy continues to rely on a handful of too-big-to-fail digital monopolies, we will have no one but ourselves to blame when our screens inevitably go black again. Andrew Cullen is a board member at Music Technology Australia, a member of the WIPO AI Technical Exchange Committee, and managing consultant at EthiCan.

articles.content: Daniel Featherstone Nearly two thirds of households in remote First Nations communities do not have access to free-to-air TV, due to issues with the satellite service that delivers television where normal broadcasts are unavailable. The latest report from the Mapping the Digital Gap project also shows the use of online streaming is on the rise. But here too access can be limited and often unaffordable for First Nations people in remote communities. Without access to free-to-air TV, spending on pre-paid mobile data may rise, mobile services can become overloaded. People may also depend more on unreliable sources of news and information. These findings are based on visits we made to 11 remote communities in 2025 and 2026. They build on research conducted since 2022 covering digital access, affordability, digital ability and access to media and information services. Why free-to-air TV matters First Nations radio and TV services, such as NITV and Indigenous Community TV, provide trusted, place-based and relevant news, information and language content. Yet access to these services is restricted by issues with VAST, broadcast maintenance, and the changing ways audiences access news. The Australian government has committed to ensuring Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples achieve equal levels of digital inclusion by 2026. This means they would have access to information and services enabling participation and informed decision-making about their own lives. The VAST service In many remote communities, people access free-to-air TV via the federal government’s Viewer Access Satellite Television (VAST) service. VAST began rolling out in 2010 as analogue TV broadcasts were switched off in favour of digital. Direct-to-home satellite equipment was installed in most remote First Nations households from 2011 to 2013. This replaced community broadcasting in many sites. However, households now have to maintain this equipment. Failure of set-top boxes is common due to power surges. Smart cards needed for access are also often removed. Satellite dishes and cabling also fail due to damage or deterioration. Radio and VAST services rely on satellite connectivity. Extreme weather conditions such as cyclones, storms and heavy cloud cover can also affect satellite connections. This can leave households without information services during weather emergencies. A system breaking down – and it’s hard to repair In remote communities, technical support typically comes from regional centres which makes maintenance more difficult and costly. A new set-top box typically costs between $400 and $600 in local stores, which can be a significant cost. People also report difficulties with activating smart cards. We found 63% of our survey respondents had no access to free-to-air TV, up from 50% in 2022. Some remote communities report an even higher than average failure rate of VAST set-top boxes. In Ampilatwatja, only 24% of VAST TV services were working. Results were similar in Pipalyatjara and Kalka (both 25%), despite satellite dish upgrades on houses in remote South Australia by Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Housing. VAST TV rates were also low for Utju (32%), Maningrida (34%) and Woorabinda (38%) in 2026, with Warakurna also on 34% in 2025. In October, the First Nations Digital Inclusion Advisory Group called for upgrades to VAST services and a return to community broadcasting. Community-led solutions To improve free-to-air TV access, two small communities have initiated community-led solutions to reduce set-top box costs and card activation issues. In Oak Valley, where local staff assist residents to activate set-top boxes, 64% of residents have access to TV services in 2026. In Punmu, the community provides residents set-top boxes with pre-activated smart cards at wholesale prices, and we found 82% of survey respondents have working VAST TV services in 2026, up from 62% in 2025. Drawing on previous research from the Mapping the Digital Gap project, the NT government recently funded a three-year trial upgrade of TV broadcasting in three Central Australian regional councils. This provides a pilot case study for a potential national upgrade program. The latest report’s findings also highlight that households are taking up fixed broadband rapidly, up from 8% in 2025 to 32% in 2026, including 24% with Starlink services. This suggests people want to access TV and other digital content on demand, and streaming services are becoming more popular across communities as local media services become more limited. Overall, there remains a high reliance on prepaid data in remote communities with 93% owning or sharing a mobile phone and 98% of these on pre-paid plans. Despite the high fixed broadband uptake, an average of 88% of communications spending in remote First Nations households goes to prepaid mobile recharges. A federal government-funded rollout of free community-wide Wi-Fi networks to 23 remote communities across Australia since 2024-25 is helping to address access and affordability challenges in those sites. A second-phase rollout to 52 communities and homelands is also under way. These and other initiatives led by governments, industry and communities are helping to close the digital gap for remote First Nations communities. The authors would like to acknowledge co-authors Julian Thomas, Jenny Kennedy, Leah Hawkins, Yee Man Louie, Alison Barton, Shane Bawden and Lauren Ganley for their work on the 2026 Mapping the Digital Gap Outcomes Report. The Mapping the Digital Gap research project is being undertaken within the ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making and Society, and receives funding from industry partner Telstra and the Australian Research Council. Daniel also co-leads an Australian Government funded national project to measure digital inclusion for First Nations Australians. Daniel is a member of the Expert Panel of the First Nations Digital Inclusion Advisory Board. He is a Director of the Australian Communications Consumer Action Network (ACCAN) and was formerly General Manager of First Nations Media Australia. Lyndon Ormond-Parker is a Principal Research Fellow on the Mapping the Digital Gap project, which receives funding from Telstra and the Australian Research Council. He also currently holds a part-time ARC Discovery Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Award with the Centre for Heritage and Museum Studies, Australian National University. Lyndon is also co-chair of the First Nations Digital Inclusion Advisory Group. articles.content: On Friday, all flights across the United States were grounded for more than four hours due to what appeared to be a telecommunications issue . The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued an alert citing “ extraordinary circumstances ” and called for all departing flights to remain ground stopped until further notice. According to media reports, about 3,500 flights were in the air when the alert was issued – all landed safely. With thousands of flights delayed and cancelled, millions of passengers were stranded in airports. The travel disruptions have been slowly resolving over the weekend. The ground stop was attributed to an update to air traffic control equipment during planned maintenance. So what exactly happened? What caused it? US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy attributed the disruption to maintenance undertaken by government contractor L3Harris at a remote FAA facility . The work involved replacing copper telecommunications wires with fibre-optic links, as well as changing how the system sends signals from an older method known as time-division multiplexing (TDM) to the more recent internet protocol (IP). During this maintenance, a router (a networking device) reportedly generated more than 1,000 connection requests every four to five seconds. This affected other routers on the network, disrupting aircraft communications and some radar data feeds. Duffy described the upgrade as a transition from analogue to digital technology , but this conflates different aspects of telecommunications. Copper and fibre describe the physical medium carrying signals, while TDM and IP describe how information is transmitted and organised. Copper cables can carry digital data, and TDM is widely used in digital telecommunications. Fibre-optic systems also carry digital data, using light rather than electrical signals. Consequently, replacing copper with fibre doesn’t necessarily mean a change from analogue to digital. The more significant change is the method for sending signals. With TDM, the system sends information through a single channel at fixed time slots, a bit like letting through traffic across a single-lane bridge at set intervals. By contrast, an IP network can carry information in packets along many paths, which improves flexibility and how much data the network can handle. However, it also changes how the equipment interacts – and what can happen in case of a fault. If not isolated in time, a malfunctioning router can affect other equipment connected to the same network. On fibre, excessive connection requests will travel more freely. Why would a network disruption ground planes? Air traffic controllers use surveillance and radio communications to make sure planes travel smoothly and stay out of each other’s way. Radar and satellite-based surveillance provide aircraft positions, while communications allow controllers to issue instructions and coordinate movements between control centres. All this relies on telecommunications networks connecting facilities across the country. Aircraft can navigate independently during a network failure, but controllers can’t safely manage the usual volume of flights if the comms are not fully reliable. The precise cause of why the router sent so many requests remains under investigation . Incorrect installation, configuration errors, and defective equipment are all potential explanations, and we’ll have to wait and see. A nationwide ground stop following a technical failure is not unprecedented. In January 2023, a malfunction of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system, which supplies pilots with operational information, also suspended departures across the United States . Although these two failures involved different systems, both show that a national aviation network that shares services throughout can be broadly impacted in case of a fault. Was this related to Microsoft or AI? The incident prompted speculation about it being linked to the global Microsoft outage that occurred just the day before. Another suggestion was that the fault might lay with the FAA’s recently announced expansion of SMART , an artificial intelligence-assisted traffic management system. Both Microsoft and Air Space Intelligence, the company responsible for SMART, have denied involvement . Officials also noted that the maintenance of the network was completely separate from this air traffic control modernisation program. What can be done to prevent this happening again? In September 2026, a US government report classified 51 of the FAA’s 138 air traffic control systems as unsustainable, and another 54 as potentially unsustainable. The FAA is actively working on replacing ageing communications, radar, and control equipment. However, modernisation introduces additional risks. When you add a new technology to the system, not only do you need to fit it with existing infrastructure, but you also need to maintain operations. To prevent ground stops like the one this week, the FAA will need to do more than replacing cables or purchasing equipment. If they segment the network, faults won’t travel as far. With proper configuration, they can ensure communications don’t get overloaded if a similar router error were to happen. The ground stop was a good measure to ensure safety when the comms failed. But a resilient aviation system must not only respond safely to equipment failures, but also prevent localised faults from disrupting national operations. The work involved replacing copper telecommunications wires with fibre-optic links, as well as changing how the system sends signals from an older method known as time-division multiplexing (TDM) to the more recent internet protocol (IP). During this maintenance, a router (a networking device) reportedly generated more than 1,000 connection requests every four to five seconds. This affected other routers on the network, disrupting aircraft communications and some radar data feeds. Duffy described the upgrade as a transition from analogue to digital technology , but this conflates different aspects of telecommunications. Copper and fibre describe the physical medium carrying signals, while TDM and IP describe how information is transmitted and organised. Copper cables can carry digital data, and TDM is widely used in digital telecommunications. Fibre-optic systems also carry digital data, using light rather than electrical signals. Consequently, replacing copper with fibre doesn’t necessarily mean a change from analogue to digital. The more significant change is the method for sending signals. With TDM, the system sends information through a single channel at fixed time slots, a bit like letting through traffic across a single-lane bridge at set intervals. By contrast, an IP network can carry information in packets along many paths, which improves flexibility and how much data the network can handle. However, it also changes how the equipment interacts – and what can happen in case of a fault. If not isolated in time, a malfunctioning router can affect other equipment connected to the same network. On fibre, excessive connection requests will travel more freely. Why would a network disruption ground planes? Air traffic controllers use surveillance and radio communications to make sure planes travel smoothly and stay out of each other’s way. Radar and satellite-based surveillance provide aircraft positions, while communications allow controllers to issue instructions and coordinate movements between control centres. All this relies on telecommunications networks connecting facilities across the country. Aircraft can navigate independently during a network failure, but controllers can’t safely manage the usual volume of flights if the comms are not fully reliable. The precise cause of why the router sent so many requests remains under investigation . Incorrect installation, configuration errors, and defective equipment are all potential explanations, and we’ll have to wait and see. A nationwide ground stop following a technical failure is not unprecedented. In January 2023, a malfunction of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system, which supplies pilots with operational information, also suspended departures across the United States . Although these two failures involved different systems, both show that a national aviation network that shares services throughout can be broadly impacted in case of a fault. Was this related to Microsoft or AI? The incident prompted speculation about it being linked to the global Microsoft outage that occurred just the day before. Another suggestion was that the fault might lay with the FAA’s recently announced expansion of SMART , an artificial intelligence-assisted traffic management system. Both Microsoft and Air Space Intelligence, the company responsible for SMART, have denied involvement . Officials also noted that the maintenance of the network was completely separate from this air traffic control modernisation program. What can be done to prevent this happening again? In September 2026, a US government report classified 51 of the FAA’s 138 air traffic control systems as unsustainable, and another 54 as potentially unsustainable. The FAA is actively working on replacing ageing communications, radar, and control equipment. However, modernisation introduces additional risks. When you add a new technology to the system, not only do you need to fit it with existing infrastructure, but you also need to maintain operations. To prevent ground stops like the one this week, the FAA will need to do more than replacing cables or purchasing equipment. If they segment the network, faults won’t travel as far. With proper configuration, they can ensure communications don’t get overloaded if a similar router error were to happen. The ground stop was a good measure to ensure safety when the comms failed. But a resilient aviation system must not only respond safely to equipment failures, but also prevent localised faults from disrupting national operations. articles.content: Angel Bena/Pexels Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill. According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X , the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”. In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems. This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters. Beyond missed emails or workplace meetings The list of services Microsoft says are “potentially impacted” by the outage is long. It includes services used for email, document sharing, meetings and managing tasks, such as Outlook, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Planner and Microsoft Exchange Online. It also includes Microsoft Defender, a cloud-based cybersecurity service. With so many digital services affected, the real-world impacts of the outage have been widespread, and go far beyond missed emails or workplace meetings. For example, family violence workers reportedly can’t access databases which contain client details. Schools can’t provide online lessons for remote students. Psychologists can’t provide telehealth consultations. Businesses are unable to process orders. Job hunters are unable to make it to planned interviews. Some government service centres have been forced to closed. The disruption also reached services outside Microsoft . OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with the tools that connect their artificial intelligence (AI) services to Microsoft 365. This shows how a problem in one part of the digital world can affect tools that appear separate, and even services provided by other companies. The outage comes after other disruptions to Microsoft services earlier this year. For example, in January, Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were down for hours. Then in August, Microsoft Outlook and Exchange Online were disrupted by a code update which took several days to fix. A shifting account of what went wrong As of early Friday afternoon Sydney time, Microsoft has not yet named a root cause of the outage, and its account of the failure has shifted since it was first reported . Initially the company said elevated load across multiple regions was reported first. It then clarified the load was not driven by an increase in traffic, but a large number of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable. Attention then moved to the automated “health checks” Microsoft uses to judge whether a server is fit to carry traffic, and to the component that processes them. The company described a core process on the affected servers as becoming “overwhelmed”. Software deployments and configuration changes were paused while recent changes were reviewed, although none was found to correlate with the start of the disruption. The evidence does not suggest a cyberattack. A distributed denial-of-service attack works by flooding a service with requests from outside until legitimate ones can no longer be answered. Microsoft’s own statement that overall traffic had not increased is difficult to reconcile with that pattern. No evidence of malicious activity has been disclosed, and no group has claimed responsibility. Indeed, Microsoft said : “There’s no indication this is a cyber attack.” The more mundane explanation fits better. Health checks exist to protect a service by withdrawing servers that appear unwell. When the machinery making that judgement is itself at fault, healthy capacity can be removed, and the servers that remain are left to absorb work they were never sized for. Outages of this scale are more often self-inflicted in this way than they are the work of attackers, as the August disruption to Microsoft email by a code update illustrates. Until a post-incident review is published, however, that remains an inference drawn from Microsoft’s own updates rather than a settled account. Microsoft has not yet been able to fix the outage entirely. It says that some of the affected servers are working again , but they “can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic”. Planning for outages like we do for bushfires This outage reinforces the need for all of us to better prepare for digital outages. For individuals, this can involve storing essential information, such as contacts and medical prescriptions, offline in case of an outage. Organisations that rely on one digital provider such as Microsoft or Google for tasks must also prepare back up plans. Crucially, they must also test these back plans to make sure they work in practice and don’t simply exist on paper – similar to how they conduct fire drills and how communities practice bushfire evacuations. As more aspects of our lives become connected – from cars and homes to workplaces, transport and healthcare – and AI becomes more widely used, the consequences of digital disruption may grow. Building resilience must be part of how we plan for that future. articles.content: A stone tool found in the desert. Chris Clarkson A fossil hippo tooth is an unlikely find in the middle of a desert. The vast sandy expanse of Arabia’s Empty Quarter or Rub’ al Khali stretches across the southern part of the peninsula, covering parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, Yemen and the United Arab Emirates. Yet its ancient sands preserve evidence of a very different landscape. About 125,000 years ago, a freshwater lake filled the Mundafan basin in southern Saudi Arabia. Hippos lived in its waters, while giant buffalo, gazelles and oryx roamed the surrounding grasslands. People lived and worked along the shore, leaving behind stone tools that still preserve microscopic traces of their activities. Our new study, published in Science , reveals how these people made hunting weapons and processed plants. Chemical traces on some stone points suggest they used plant poisons to hunt. These findings offer a rare view of life in Arabia during an early period of human expansion beyond Africa. They help us understand the skills and resources that allowed humans to live in a place now dominated by desert. Rub’ al Khali desert stretches across the Arabian Peninsula. Google Maps (2026) Beyond Africa Our species evolved in Africa, where fossils show early Homo sapiens existed by about 300,000 years ago . Our subsequent expansion into other continents involved repeated movements, with many questions about their timing and consequences still unresolved. Fossils show our species reached parts of Asia well before the major expansion about 60–70,000 years ago . Homo sapiens fossils in Greece and Israel , for example, place our species outside of Africa by about 200,000 years ago, while a human finger bone from northern Arabia places Homo sapiens on the Arabian peninsula at least 85,000 years ago. Researchers continue to debate which routes people took and how these earlier populations relate to later ones. Arabia occupies a central position between Africa and Asia. Earlier research documents repeated human occupation over the past 400,000 years, involving different human groups during wetter climatic phases. These periods of “Green Arabia” created lakes and grasslands within today’s deserts. Our study examines how people lived in one such environment. Evidence on stone-tipped weapons Our international team investigated ‘Uruq Aljelibah, beside the ancient Mundafan lake. We collected more than 5,500 stone tools and pieces left from making them, and mapped their positions alongside animal fossils. Some flakes refit together, helping us identify places where people made tools. A hippo tooth from ‘Uruq Aljelibah. Chris Clarkson We dated the lake and shoreline deposits using luminescence dating – measuring signals in buried sand grains that record the time since sunlight last reached them. These results, supported by data on hippo teeth, place the archaeological shoreline at about 125,000 years ago. Microscopic examination revealed broken tips on several stone points, consistent with impact during hunting. One point preserved resin and plant fibres near its base, suggesting people glued and bound it to a shaft. Animal fats and protein survived nearer the tip. Together, these traces support its use as a hunting weapon, although we can’t determine whether someone threw it or thrust it. Left to right: saw-toothed ‘denticulate’ used to process plants including palm; a retouched stone point; a tool produced with the unique Levallois technique. Chris Clarkson Chemical analysis revealed traces linked to the arrow-poison tree, whose toxins affect the heart. On at least one impact-damaged point, there were potentially toxic plant compounds alongside animal residues. Other tools carried traces consistent with extracting and processing toxic plant latex. These finds show humans used poison-assisted hunting about 65,000 years earlier than recently reported South African examples. Plants were part of the toolkit Other tools preserved fragments of leaves, wood and fibres, including tissue from bark and palm leaves. We also found traces of reeds and underground plant parts. Fibres and wear on tools with toothed edges suggest people sawed or shredded plants, potentially producing material for bindings and other equipment. Wood and fibre usually disappear from the archaeological record. Their surviving traces help us reconstruct parts of ancient technology that stone alone cannot reveal, including weapon shafts and possible cord or containers. Plants provided materials that could serve many purposes. Gilbert Price from the University of Queensland and Paul Breeze from Kings College London excavating ‘Hetti’ the hippo. Chris Clarkson We also found animal fossils, which help to reconstruct the environment around the lake. Hippos indicate substantial freshwater habitat, while giant buffalo, gazelles, oryx and ostriches point to open grasslands nearby. Together, they suggest a landscape that offered people water and a range of potential prey. Animal remains also cluster in areas with high concentrations of stone tools, linking some lakeshore activities to the fauna. This association supports the evidence that the humans living here hunted and processed the animals they killed. An ephemeral life Mundafan filled during separate wet phases, and the opportunities it offered changed as the climate became drier. We don’t yet know where its inhabitants went. What their tools reveal is how knowledge of local plants and animals helped people occupy a landscape that was later abandoned as the lake dried and deserts returned. Mundafan offers us a glimpse of an early stage in the human journey beyond Africa, with later traces of Homo sapiens documenting our species’ widening presence in China, Laos, Indonesia and, by about 65,000 years ago, Australia. The authors would like to acknowledge the Saudi Heritage Commission, particularly Faisal Al-Jibreen and his team; Frans van Buchem and Laurence Hapiot of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology; and Abdullah Alsharekh of King Saud University for their invaluable collaboration and contributions to this research. articles.content: Curtin University , CC BY Since 2022, astronomers have been puzzling over a new kind of cosmic object called long-period radio transients . These are objects that emit bright flashes of radio waves into space every few minutes to every few hours. Some have been traced back to binary systems of a small, dim cool star called a red dwarf in orbit with a star remnant called a white dwarf. In new research published today in Nature Astronomy, we report the first discovery of a different source for one of these enigmatic intermittent broadcasters: it still involves a white dwarf, but also a star much like our own Sun. The search for sources After the discovery of the first long-period radio transient in 2022, once we had ruled out aliens , we went looking for natural explanations. One idea was that they were extremely slow-spinning neutron star pulsars, the collapsed cores of enormous stars which also send out repeating radio flashes. But in theory a neutron star spinning that slowly shouldn’t produce radio waves, so the answer had to be something else. When we started traced these radio signals back to their sources, we made a breakthrough. One of our repeating signals came from a red dwarf star, probably orbiting a white dwarf (the remnant of a star like our Sun). Across the handful of long-period transients whose source stars we can identify, a pattern has emerged: a binary system of a white dwarf and a small, cool red dwarf. The source of the newly discovered long-period radio transient is precisely located to a G-type star like the Sun. Stellarium / PanSTARRS , CC BY A signal from the wrong kind of star In late 2024, we were looking for new long-period transients using the Murchison Widefield Array radio telescope in Western Australia. Using a search method developed by PhD student Csanád Horváth , we spotted something: short flashes of radio waves, arriving like clockwork every 7.9 minutes. Then the flashes stopped. For weeks we saw nothing, and we nearly gave up. But when we plotted every detection and non-detection together, a pattern emerged. The pulses only appear during a window of about six hours, followed by 26 hours without pulses. The most natural explanation is that the system is a binary: two stars orbiting each other once every 32 hours, with the radio pulses only visible when they are lined up in the right way . The MeerKAT telescope in South Africa pinpointed the source to a tiny patch of sky containing a single faint star. We turned to the Keck telescope in Hawai’i to record the star’s spectrum – the “fingerprint” of its light, which can tell us a lot about the star itself. The result was a surprise: this was not a tiny red dwarf, but a G-type star almost the same mass and temperature as our own Sun. How we discovered the new object, and how it connects to long-period radio transients. Weighing a star we can’t see How can we be sure our source isn’t a neutron star after all? The clue is in the timing. As the pulsing object swings around its orbit, the pulses arrive up to four seconds earlier or later than expected, because the radio waves have further to travel at some points than others. That tells us how large the orbit is. The precise spectrum “fingerprint” of the Sun-like star shows it barely wobbles as the pulsing object orbits around it. This means the Sun-like star must be much heavier than its partner. When we combine the calculation of the size of the orbit, how long each orbit takes, and the spectrum measurements, we can work out that the pulsing object is about two-thirds as heavy as the Sun. That means it’s too light to be a neutron star. We believe the pulsing object is a white dwarf pulsar, the first found in orbit around a Sun-like star. What strange systems are hiding in the dark? How did this odd couple come to be? We think the star that became the white dwarf must have first swelled into a giant, engulfing its companion, which spiralled inward and shrank the orbit before the giant’s outer layers were ejected. We think systems like this are probably quite common in the universe, but white dwarfs next to bright stars are very hard to see. The glare of the bright star hides the faint white dwarf. Radio pulses, on the other hand, cut through the glare. If more long-period transients turn out to be hiding white dwarfs around bright stars, radio surveys could uncover a whole undiscovered population that optical and X-ray telescopes miss. This is important because some white dwarf binaries are thought to be the ancestors of Type Ia supernovae. Astronomers use these exploding stars as “standard candles” – reference points to measure interstellar distances and the expansion of the universe. Finding these systems could reveal more about this process. With the next generation of radio telescopes, such as the SKA Observatory , we expect to find many more. And if we can find these objects around many different types of stars, it will give us insights into the lives and deaths of stars like our own Sun, across our galaxy and beyond. When we combine the calculation of the size of the orbit, how long each orbit takes, and the spectrum measurements, we can work out that the pulsing object is about two-thirds as heavy as the Sun. That means it’s too light to be a neutron star. We believe the pulsing object is a white dwarf pulsar, the first found in orbit around a Sun-like star. What strange systems are hiding in the dark? How did this odd couple come to be? We think the star that became the white dwarf must have first swelled into a giant, engulfing its companion, which spiralled inward and shrank the orbit before the giant’s outer layers were ejected. We think systems like this are probably quite common in the universe, but white dwarfs next to bright stars are very hard to see. The glare of the bright star hides the faint white dwarf. Radio pulses, on the other hand, cut through the glare. If more long-period transients turn out to be hiding white dwarfs around bright stars, radio surveys could uncover a whole undiscovered population that optical and X-ray telescopes miss. This is important because some white dwarf binaries are thought to be the ancestors of Type Ia supernovae. Astronomers use these exploding stars as “standard candles” – reference points to measure interstellar distances and the expansion of the universe. Finding these systems could reveal more about this process. With the next generation of radio telescopes, such as the SKA Observatory , we expect to find many more. And if we can find these objects around many different types of stars, it will give us insights into the lives and deaths of stars like our own Sun, across our galaxy and beyond. articles.content: EHT Collaboration On April 10 2019, the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) Collaboration revealed the first picture of a black hole . The object is at the centre of a galaxy known as M87, about 55 million light-years away. The iconic ring structure instantly became one of the most recognised scientific images of the modern era. It showed a black hole “shadow” outlined by light from swirling hot gas – just as predicted by Einstein’s theory of general relativity. The result supported the long-standing idea that the centres of galaxies house supermassive black holes. However, scientists have since had some disagreements on whether the details and structure of the ring in the original publication were accurate. Our new research, published today in Nature , used new techniques to investigate the original datasets. Not only do our results validate the original work, but they also provide a fresh perspective on the ring structure. Our independent results enhance confidence in one of the most significant modern scientific results. And we bring the image of a black hole millions of light-years away back into focus. A small team of four from Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO, have confirmed the iconic 2019 black hole image. From left to right: Ivy Wong, Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, Samuel Lai and Foivos Diakogiannis. CSIRO An Earth-sized telescope Imaging the supermassive black hole at the centre of galaxy M87 is very challenging. It’s similar to photographing a doughnut on the Moon while standing on Earth. To obtain that level of sharpness and detail, you’d need a telescope the size of the entire planet. To achieve this, the EHT combined signals from radio telescopes across the globe. Doing so enabled the sharpest imaging possible from down here on Earth. The results ushered in a new era of imaging – we could finally see the extreme environments around black holes. Four independent imaging teams within the EHT Collaboration participated in the original publication. Though all teams produced a ring-like structure , there were some differences in how the black hole’s fine-scale features were represented. Such differences are known to be caused by human and algorithmic biases in the imaging process. However, one study fundamentally challenged the ring-like nature of the source. Some discrepancies are understandable. They’re bound to happen when combining data from a sparse telescope array into one Earth-sized virtual telescope. Other factors contribute, too. Each radio telescope gathering the data will also introduce errors, caused by its instruments or simply by Earth’s atmosphere. Normally, astronomers estimate these errors and correct them during the analysis. But residual errors from this complex process can lead to incorrect outcomes. To address these issues, we developed a new method for combining data, called “ closure invariants ”. The standard practice for analysing the data combines pairs of telescope measurements. By contrast, closure invariants combine triplets – three telescope measurements at once. This not only eliminates those atmospheric and instrumental errors, it also reveals cleaner information about the object’s structure. Simulated video of emission surrounding the supermassive black hole at the centre of galaxy M87, morphed into our GenDIReCT reconstruction on the April 21 2018 dataset. Video created by S. Lai, N. Thyagarajan, O. I. Wong, and F. Diakogiannis (CSIRO). Rendered using the ipole algorithm (Mościbrodzka & Gammie, 2018) with simulation data provided by the University of Illinois (Dhruv et al. 2025) The face of a black hole To make the most of the data from our closure invariants, we designed a machine learning imaging method called GenDIReCT , which produces images consistent with the measured data. To minimise biases, we trained it on terrestrial images like cats, dogs, and cars. Therefore, it had no idea what a black hole looked like. We also put the model through a large suite of validation tests, which included imaging a wide range of non-ring structures. This included validation on real datasets of other galaxies like Centaurus A. Once satisfied with its accuracy, we froze the training and testing procedure so human biases couldn’t affect our imaging outcomes. On December 4 2025, we finally allowed our fully validated imaging method to “look” at the EHT observations of M87. Across all datasets, the ring structure was consistent. The appearance and diameter of the ring were consistent with a black hole with a mass of 6.5 billion Suns observed nearly face-on – like looking straight down into the eye of a hurricane. A fresh perspective When compared directly to images from the EHT collaboration, our result is consistent in diameter and overall orientation. Naturally, there are some differences in the fine details of ring width and surface brightness along the circumference, but the overall structure matches. This provides a fresh perspective on the iconic black hole ring while also resolving previous discrepancies. To prove this success didn’t depend solely on advanced machine learning, we also developed a complementary imaging method based on traditional statistical techniques. This entirely different method also validated our structure using the new closure invariant data we produced. Overall, our work delivers a strong independent validation of the supermassive black hole structure at the centre of galaxy M87. And it could do more in the future. Our technique could also be useful in other situations where data from multiple sensors are combined to map unknown structures – such as medical imaging or mapping earthquakes. articles.content: energyy/Getty Images Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has just announced six mandatory artificial intelligence (AI) safety guardrails. The government will establish a new AI safety regulator to enforce the regulations, with the power to impose significant penalties. According to the guardrails, frontier AI companies – the ones with the most powerful AI models at the cutting edge of AI development – will have to: implement security controls identify and manage serious risks allow independent evaluation of their models rapidly notify government of serious incidents publish safety and security frameworks to enhance governance and transparency respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change. The implementation of the guardrails is one of 18 recommendations from a rapid review the government launched in September after an AI agent, deployed by OpenAI to collect data, accessed non-public Medicare stats . In the background, the government is pursuing an extensive agenda of technology law and policy reform. There’s a new prohibition on unfair trading practices focused on online markets, a digital duty of care bill to address harms from online platforms and AI chatbots, a significant draft privacy law reform bill , and an inquiry into Australia’s sovereign AI capability. The prime minister’s announcement focuses on “AI safety”, “AI security” and “frontier” AI models and companies. But Australians may remain unprotected from known AI harms that – though less spectacular – are already widespread and serious. A diversified approach to AI policy and regulation As well as the mandatory guardrails, the rapid review recommendations included criminal law reform, international cooperation, and strengthening mechanisms for government engagement with frontier AI developers. Nearly half of the recommendations are about increasing Australia’s preparedness for AI-related cyber incidents. The recommendations make sense. The review is right to emphasise the role of building capacity, relationships, and cooperation. Effective and responsive AI regulation must go beyond the government simply issuing and enforcing rigid rules. Despite these strengths, the government seems to be taking a narrow view of what “AI safety” means. What counts as AI safety? The announcement seems to indicate that the most important risks come from frontier AI models. But risks from AI – including serious risks to safety, public health and national security – are not confined to the frontier. AI and algorithmic systems are increasingly integrated into important services such as healthcare, insurance, housing, finance, employment, education and social security. For the most part, these kinds of AI systems are not likely to be frontier AI. Instead, these would be smaller, more specialised tools, such as an AI recruitment bot, an AI personal budgeting app or an educational grading algorithm . Unaccountable, unfair, poorly managed deployments of such everyday AI systems have the potential to cause enormous harm. We’ve seen Robodebt harm hundreds of thousands of Australians. Sexist AI-enabled job recruitment tools , AI-enabled stadium security systems that let a gun into the Melbourne Cricket Ground, racist policing algorithms , and AI meal-planners that recommend poisonous recipes are just a few among thousands of examples of everyday AI harms and risks. As the Medicare incident showed, risks also emerge from interactions between software systems, organisations and real world contexts. It doesn’t make sense to just focus on powerful AI models out of context. Worse, AI systems are notoriously opaque . While changes to privacy law will soon require businesses and government to state in their privacy policies if they use automated decision-making, Australians don’t have a right to an actual explanation of AI decisions in most domains. A lack of transparency about how (non-frontier) AI systems are developed and deployed is a serious impediment to accountability . A lighter touch The Australian government recognised all of this in an earlier 2024 proposal for mandatory AI guardrails. However, these have largely been abandoned in favour of a lighter regulatory touch. The 2024 proposal contemplated ten guardrails that would apply to non-frontier AI systems deployed in high-risk settings, as well as frontier systems. These would have included requirements for transparency, accountability, testing, data governance, record keeping, risk management, human oversight of systems, and pathways for contesting AI decisions. Most of those guardrails are missing from the new list. Now, only safety frameworks need to be transparent, for instance. Independent oversight seems limited to evaluating AI models themselves, rather than evaluating whether the development and deployment of AI systems in various contexts is safe, fair, responsible or accountable. There are also no general record-keeping or transparency guardrails that would create the paper trails we need for real oversight and accountability. Some promising changes One area that looks promising is the requirement to respond to new standards and rules. Depending on how the guardrails are implemented, standards such as Australia’s nuanced and sophisticated Voluntary AI Safety Standard could provide more detailed guidance to promote fairness, transparency and accountability. If compliance with certain standards were mandated, then guardrails could have a deeper and wider reach. Similarly, a proposal to introduce criminal liability for negligent AI developers could incentivise better record-keeping and more proactive risk management. But until the government fleshes out this bullet point list of guardrails and rapid review recommendations, it will be hard to know how broad the scope of AI safety regulation will be. For now, one thing is clear. Introducing regulation for sci-fi frontier risks such as “rogue” AI agents attacking our government or infrastructure is good politics, and sound policy. But it’s not enough to keep Australians safe from serious AI harms.
